findings.headline: Meridian Water phasing review in progress; completion dates will significantly affect MRP and CFR
findings.detail: The council is conducting a review of Meridian Water's next development phases. Timing of the outcome will material affect MRP forecasts and capital financing requirement. Earlier parcel completion increases near-term costs; delays increase risk of breaching the £997m General Fund CFR ceiling.
findings.matters: This is a known variable affecting debt forecasts; any material re-phasing could require revised borrowing plans and could trigger stress on the GF CFR limit which already shows tight headroom.
findings.figures: GF CFR limit: £997m; current forecast: £955.5m
findings.quote: A review of the next phases of Meridian Water is in progress. Once completed MRP forecasts will be reviewed to ensure prudent provision continues in accordance with the Council's MRP Policy.

findings.headline: NLWA waste authority debt generates £181m contingent liability exposure for Enfield
findings.detail: North London Waste Authority holds £1.27bn in debt and is refinancing short-term loans to longer-term instruments when market rates permit. Enfield, as one of seven boroughs, faces a contingent liability of approximately £181m (its one-seventh share) which will be recovered via waste gate fees.
findings.matters: This contingent debt obligation will eventually flow through to council residents via waste charges, reducing Enfield's capacity to manage other budget pressures or rates.
findings.figures: NLWA total debt: £1.27bn; Enfield potential share (1/7): ~£181m
findings.quote: NLWA currently has £1.27bn of debt which is £230m below the Authorised Limit of £1.5bn. NLWA borrowing is in the form of short-term maturity loans which will be re-financed to longer term products when rates permit.

findings.headline: NHS ICB owes council £11.1m, reducing available liquidity
findings.detail: As at 30 June 2026, the Integrated Care Board (NHS) owed Enfield £11.1m. This represents ~9.5% of the council's £116.7m cash investments and reflects working capital strain on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Significant NHS debt reduces immediate liquidity and reflects wider NHS cash pressures; if recovery is delayed, this could force the council to adjust working capital management or increase short-term borrowing.
findings.figures: ICB debt: £11.1m; council cash investments: £116.7m
findings.quote: For example, as at 30 June 2026, the ICB (part of the NHS) owes the Council £11.1m.

findings.headline: Energetik loans generating £1.2m impairment charges, with only £1.9m reserve coverage
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £1.2m in impairment charges for 2026/27, primarily attributable to Energetik. Against £57.4m of Energetik loans outstanding, the council holds an earmarked reserve of only £1.9m to absorb future credit losses.
findings.matters: Impairment charges signal deteriorating credit quality on major loans to subsidiaries; reserve coverage of 3.3% leaves material exposure if Energetik's position worsens further.
findings.figures: Energetik loans balance: £57.4m; impairment charges 2026/27: £1.2m; earmarked reserve: £1.9m
findings.quote: Despite all loans being considered recoverable, these charges (termed impairments or expected credit losses depending on the loan type) are estimated at £1.2m for 2026/27 and relate mainly to Energetik.

findings.headline: HRA concessionary borrowing rate (40bps discount) expires March 2027, raising future borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council currently benefits from a 40bps discount on HRA borrowing rates under a concessionary arrangement that terminates 31 March 2027. After that date, HRA will borrow at full market rates, increasing debt servicing costs precisely when the ICR is already stressed.
findings.matters: The loss of this rate advantage will increase HRA debt costs at a time when interest cover is already forecast below minimum. Combined with rising ICR stress and LTV, this creates a squeeze on HRA debt affordability.
findings.figures: HRA concessionary rate discount: 40bps; expiry date: 31 March 2027
findings.quote: A further discount of 40 bps is available when accessing the HRA concessionary rate in place until March 2027 which the Council has taken advantage of for HRA borrowing.

findings.headline: HRA Loan to Value exceeds maximum target at 55%, up from 49% last year
findings.detail: Forecast HRA debt relative to asset base is 55%, exceeding the council's maximum prudential target of 51.6%. This signals increasing HRA leverage and debt-to-assets ratio, a reversal of prior improvement.
findings.matters: Rising LTV indicates HRA debt is growing faster than assets; for a lender, this reduces loan coverage and increases refinance risk if asset values fall or revenue pressures mount.
findings.figures: LTV 2025/26: 49.0%; 2026/27 estimate: 55.0%; maximum target: 51.6%
findings.quote: Loan to Value (LTV) Measures the level of debt compared to HRA Fixed asset valuation at year end of financial year... 2025/26: 49.0%, 2026/27 Estimate: 55.0%, maximum 51.6%

findings.headline: HRA Interest Cover Ratio forecast at 1.25, below minimum prudential target of 1.95
findings.detail: The ratio measuring HRA operating surplus adequacy to cover interest costs has fallen from 1.71 in 2025/26 to a forecast 1.25 in 2026/27. This indicates HRA debt is becoming less affordable relative to revenue and falls 36% short of the council's minimum target threshold.
findings.matters: For a lender to the HRA, declining interest cover indicates weakening debt sustainability; at 1.25x, HRA revenue surplus covers only slightly more than interest costs, leaving little buffer for service pressures or revenue shocks.
findings.figures: ICR 2025/26: 1.71; 2026/27 estimate: 1.25; minimum target: 1.95
findings.quote: Interest Cover Ratio (ICR) Measures adequacy of the in-year revenue surplus to cover interest on borrowing... 2025/26 1.71, 2026/27 Estimate 1.25, minimum 1.95

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Property and fleet maintenance backlogs emerging: £1.5m property overspend on repairs and manned security, £1.3m fleet repairs pressure
findings.detail: Property services is £1.5m overspent, with significant overspends on manned security and repairs and maintenance across the portfolio. Fleet services shows a £1.3m overspend on repairs and maintenance. Both services are 'under active review' but the paper indicates underlying maintenance pressures that suggest potential deferred maintenance or compliance issues.
findings.matters: These pressures may indicate deferred maintenance backlogs, compliance issues (particularly relevant for HRA), or service delivery challenges that could escalate if not addressed.
findings.figures: £1.5m property services overspend, £1.3m fleet repairs overspend
findings.quote: Property is adverse by £1.5m. The current forecast includes additional costs for Repairs and Maintenance across the portfolio. This is under active review with proposals to review and reduce the current programme of spend. It also includes significant overspends on Manned security.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Capital programme delivering only 79% of approved budget (£390m of £493m), with temporary accommodation leases at 50% of budget
findings.detail: The capital programme is forecast to spend £390m against an approved budget of £493.1m (79% utilisation). The most significant underspend is in General Fund temporary accommodation leases, where only £93.6m is forecast against £185.3m budgeted (50% of plan). The council notes 'unspent but committed capital budget forecast at year end will only be carried forward in exceptional circumstances and / or if grant conditions allow', suggesting pressure to reduce carried forward budgets.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage, particularly in a core strategic programme (TA leases), indicates delivery challenges and may signal reprioritisation of capital spend.
findings.figures: £390m forecast spend of £493.1m approved budget (79%), £93.6m TA leases forecast of £185.3m budgeted (50%)
findings.quote: £390.0m Q1 full year forecast against an approved budget of £493.1m...£93.6m for long-leased temporary accommodation...Unspent but committed capital budget forecast at year end will only be carried forward in exceptional circumstances and / or if grant conditions allow

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Risk reserves forecast to remain only £7.6m above minimum threshold, dependent on approval of all recommendations and delivery of mitigation actions
findings.detail: Risk reserves are forecast at £50.5m against a minimum threshold of £42.9m, providing only £7.6m of headroom. This assumes approval of all recommendations in the report and successful delivery of mitigation actions. Without these mitigations, reserves would fall to £44.5m, only £1.6m above minimum, and any further pressure would breach the threshold.
findings.matters: The council has limited buffer against further demand pressure or mitigation failure. A lender would be concerned about the tightness of reserves and the dependency on specific management actions.
findings.figures: £50.5m forecast closing balance, £42.9m minimum threshold, £44.5m without mitigations, £7.6m headroom with mitigations
findings.quote: Risk reserves based on the Q1 position are forecast to be £50.5m by year end as planned (subject to approval of recommendations in this report and subsequent Full Council approval), however there is a significant risk that without mitigating action risk reserve balances would fall below the minimum threshold.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Savings delivery materially below target: £3.7m of £18.1m planned savings deferred or undeliverable (20% shortfall)
findings.detail: Of £18.1m planned savings for 2026/27, services report that £14.4m are on track for delivery but £3.0m will be delivered later than planned and £0.7m will not be delivered in their current form. This represents a £3.7m shortfall against plan. The paper notes this is £2.2m above the £1.5m deliverability adjustment built into the budget, so a further £1m increase to the deliverability adjustment has been proposed.
findings.matters: A council forecasting balanced budgets while missing 20% of planned savings is dependent on one-off mitigations and flexibility in reserve drawdown. This suggests underlying savings programmes may not be sustainable.
findings.figures: £3.7m shortfall out of £18.1m target, £2.2m above expected deliverability adjustment, 87% delivery rate (80% without adjustment)
findings.quote: Out of £18.1m planned savings for 2026/27 (£13.4m new savings, £3.1m deferred from 2025/26 and £1.6m prior years decisions), services are reporting that £14.4m are forecast to be fully delivered, £3.0m will be delivered later than planned and £0.7m will not be delivered in their current form

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £36.1m with in-year overspend of £15.3m, costing General Fund £1m annually in interest, government support uncertain
findings.detail: The DSG is forecasting a £15.3m overspend in 2026/27, bringing the cumulative deficit to £36.1m. This deficit is costing the General Fund £1m in 2026/27 alone in interest charges. The council expects government support covering 90% of the eligible DSG deficit accrued to end of 2025/26, but 'further support is expected for deficits that arise in 2026/27 and 2027/28 however the details are still to be confirmed.' The Statutory Override ends 31 March 2028, after which the council must meet residual deficits from its own resources.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a material contingent liability. Government support is subject to conditions and approval of a local SEND reform plan. If support does not materialise, the council faces absorbing a large deficit from general resources when the override expires.
findings.figures: £36.1m cumulative deficit, £15.3m 2026/27 overspend, £1m annual interest cost, Statutory Override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG position forecast at the end of 2026/27 is £36.1m...Council's need to plan to meet the costs of the residual deficit from their own resources in 2028/29, once the statutory override ends on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Long-lease temporary accommodation scheme delivering only 332 units against 657 budgeted, escalating reliance on higher-cost temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The council budgeted to acquire 657 long-lease properties in 2026/27 but now forecasts only 332 acquisitions. The shortfall of approximately 325 units has increased reliance on higher-cost nightly-paid temporary accommodation, widening the gap between accommodation costs and rental income. The paper identifies a potential £2m risk if Long Lease supply does not improve, and notes that 'the principal risk remains the Council's ability to secure sufficient affordable accommodation to meet demand.'
findings.matters: A key mitigation strategy for homelessness costs is failing to deliver at scale. The council is reverting to higher-cost temporary accommodation, which is less financially predictable and relies on Housing Benefit subsidy rules that are constrained.
findings.figures: 332 units forecast vs 657 budgeted (50% shortfall), £2m identified risk, current £2.2m overspend on TA
findings.quote: The Lease+ programme will not however deliver the volume of properties originally anticipated and are now estimating to acquire 332 long leases. While the model remains financially advantageous compared to the use of nightly paid temporary accommodation...delivery has been constrained by the requirement to obtain individual mortgage lender consent for landlords and to register each lease with HM Land Registry.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £7.7m with forward risks of additional £3m, driven by demand growth and workforce cost inflation exceeding budget assumptions
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is £7.7m overspent against a £139.9m budget. The overspend is driven by sustained demand, increasingly complex cases, and provider fee inflation - particularly in residential and nursing care, and in Learning Disabilities transition cases where health funding ceases at age 18. The paper identifies forward risks of up to £3m if current demand trends continue, which would bring total overspend to £10.8m.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is typically the largest and most volatile pressure on council finances. This shows structural demand-led growth outpacing budget assumptions, with material unquantified risk in a demand-led service.
findings.figures: £7.7m overspend, £3m identified forward risk, £3.0m overspend in Learning Disabilities alone
findings.quote: Sustained growth in demand, increasing complexity of care needs, and inflationary pressures within the provider market continue to place considerable pressure on Adult Social Care budgets.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Revenue Capital Monitoring Report Cabinet 01.09.2026
findings.headline: General Fund revenue forecast £6m overspend, requiring £13.1m flexible use of capital receipts to balance
findings.detail: Without approved mitigations (flexible use of capital receipts and pausing further investment allocations), the council forecasts a £6m overspend. The mitigation relies on applying £13.1m of capital receipts to fund transformation costs. If these mitigations fail, risk reserves would fall to £44.5m, below the £42.9m minimum threshold.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can maintain minimum reserves and what happens if mitigation actions fail or demand pressures worsen.
findings.figures: £6m net pressure, £13.1m flexible use of capital receipts applied, risk reserves £44.5m without mitigations vs £42.9m minimum
findings.quote: A £6m net pressure is forecast that could be fully mitigated pending the approval of recommendations 2.2 and 2.3, noting continuing service pressures and risks of increase

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: External audit of internal audit found only partial conformance with audit standards
findings.detail: An external quality assessment concluded that Enfield's internal audit function only 'partially conformed' with the Global Internal Audit Standards. A Quality Assurance Improvement Programme was presented to address gaps, suggesting the internal control environment is not fully reliable.
findings.matters: Partial conformance with audit standards means the council's internal control framework has identified weaknesses that compromise assurance. This undermines confidence in how well the council can identify and manage its own risks.
findings.figures: External quality assessment finding: partial conformance (not full conformance) with standards
findings.quote: A report in June 2025 outlined the results of the External Quality Assessment which concluded that the Council partially conformed with the internal audit standards.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: £1.1m in fraud detected and prevented between April and September 2025
findings.detail: The counter fraud team identified and prevented £1.1m in fraudulent activity during a six-month period, with nine properties recovered as a result of their work. Alongside this, the audit committee approved a new Counter Fraud Strategy and Response Plan for 2025-2028.
findings.matters: The scale of fraud detected (£1.1m in six months) suggests either elevated fraud risk or improved detection; either way, it indicates governance vulnerabilities that lenders need to understand.
findings.figures: £1.1m detected and prevented fraud (April 2025 – September 2025); 9 properties recovered
findings.quote: detected and prevented fraud identified between April 2025 and September 2025 (£1.1m)

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: Energetik governance report to Cabinet lacked risk scenarios and contained potential material misstatement
findings.detail: The audit committee raised concerns about a June 2024 Cabinet report on Energetik that appeared to lack adequate risk scenarios and contain potential material misstatements. Officers agreed to inform Cabinet of these concerns. Energetik is one of the three major debt areas flagged by auditors.
findings.matters: Governance failures in reporting on a major debt/asset (Energetik) suggest weak oversight of material liabilities. This directly connects to why the auditor issued a statutory recommendation.
findings.figures: Report date: June 2024; flagged as potential material misstatement
findings.quote: Members also raised concerns about a report to Cabinet in June 2024 which appeared to contain a lack of risk scenarios and a potential material misstatement relating to Energetik.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: Risk reserve remained below minimum target, requiring boost from capital receipts to reach target within five years
findings.detail: The council's risk reserve had fallen below its minimum required level. Officers reported it had been boosted using capital receipts and was now on track to reach the minimum in the next financial year (2026-27) and the council's longer-term target within five years. This indicates the council has been drawing down reserves and is dependent on capital receipts to rebuild them.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a key indicator of financial stress. A council using capital receipts to boost reserves and taking five years to reach targets suggests structural budget challenges.
findings.figures: Risk reserve on track to reach minimum next financial year; target to be reached within 5 years
findings.quote: Officers advised that the risk reserve had been boosted with capital receipts and was now on track to reach the risk reserve minimum in the next financial year and the Council's target within 5 years.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: Financial statements for five consecutive years received disclaimer opinions from external auditor
findings.detail: The committee approved accounts for 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23 in June 2025, all with disclaimed audit opinions. The 2024-25 accounts in January 2026 were also approved in this context. Disclaimer opinions mean the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to express an opinion on whether the accounts are true and fair, indicating significant audit uncertainty.
findings.matters: A pattern of disclaimer opinions across multiple years represents a fundamental failure of audit assurance. Lenders and rating agencies treat this as a major red flag indicating the council's financial position cannot be reliably established.
findings.figures: Five years of financial statements with disclaimer opinions: 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, 2024-25
findings.quote: The Committee questioned the rationale for disclaimed opinions on each set of the Statement of Accounts

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Audit Committee Report and Review of Effectiveness
findings.headline: Auditor raised statutory recommendation in context of significant debts in HRA, Meridian Water and Energetik
findings.detail: External auditors (Grant Thornton) advised the committee that the council was in a challenging position regarding significant debts across three major areas: the Housing Revenue Account, Meridian Water, and Energetik. This context informed a statutory recommendation from the auditor, which represents formal escalation of concerns about the council's financial position and governance.
findings.matters: A statutory recommendation from external audit is a serious governance event that signals financial distress. These specific debt areas are material liabilities that directly affect lending decisions.
findings.figures: HRA debt, Meridian Water debt, Energetik debt (amounts not specified in this document)
findings.quote: Grant Thornton expressed the view that the Council was in a challenging position regarding significant debts for the HRA account, Meridian Water and Energetik and this was the context in which the Statutory Recommendation had been made.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Debt Repayment (MRP) Judgements and Choices
findings.headline: Subsidiary loan repayments are assumed; if Energetik or Housing Gateway underperform, council taxpayers may fund debt repayment instead
findings.detail: Enfield has made £199m in loans to subsidiaries (Energetik £53m, Housing Gateway Limited £146m). The council currently assumes these companies will repay, charging MRP only on expected credit losses (£483k in 2026/27). If the council instead charged MRP on all loan balances, it would be £2.512m in 2026/27 alone. This represents a contingent exposure: if subsidiaries fail to repay as expected, taxpayers absorb the debt service cost.
findings.matters: The council has a large contingent liability if subsidiaries underperform; the current MRP policy assumes company repayments but provides no quantified reserve if they fail to materialise.
findings.figures: £199m in subsidiary loans; potential MRP difference of £2.512m in 2026/27 if all loans required taxpayer-backed repayment
findings.quote: if MRP was made to provide for council-tax payer repayment on all loans, this would be circa £1.6m in 2026/27 compared to £483k estimated under the Council's policy.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Debt Repayment (MRP) Judgements and Choices
findings.headline: External audit recommended the council adopt a more conservative debt repayment method, suggesting current approach is too lenient
findings.detail: The 2024/25 external auditors estimated that switching from the annuity method (which the council uses) to equal instalments would require circa £4m higher annual MRP charges. The audit recommended the council review its approach. Using equal instalments over five years would mean £19.651m additional debt service. The council justifies annuity on intergenerational equity grounds, but audit sees it as deferring necessary costs.
findings.matters: External audit has questioned whether the council's debt repayment approach is sufficiently prudent, suggesting the audit has confidence concerns about the council's conservative posture.
findings.figures: £4m higher annual charge; £19.651m over five years
findings.quote: The 2024/25 external audit report estimated that using equal instalments method would result in a circa £4m higher Minimum Revenue Provision charge and recommended that the authority reviews its approach in this respect.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Debt Repayment (MRP) Judgements and Choices
findings.headline: CIPFA audit found MRP policy depends on council assumptions that could leave the council financially exposed if wrong
findings.detail: CIPFA's Independent Assurance Review identified the council's MRP policy as 'judgement-heavy' and dependent on assumptions about Meridian Water asset readiness, voluntary revenue provisions, and subsidiary loan recoverability. The audit noted these assumptions are permitted by regulations but 'increase exposure if assumptions are not realised.' The audit provided no quantified contingency or reserve for this exposure.
findings.matters: External audit has flagged that the council's cash set-aside for debt repayment rests on material assumptions; if these prove wrong, the council could face unquantified financial exposure and deficit risk.
findings.figures: None quantified; audit flagged Meridian Water asset readiness and subsidiary loan assumptions as particular risks
findings.quote: several elements of the policy remain judgement-heavy and depend on council-held assumptions, particularly in relation to Meridian Water asset readiness, voluntary revenue provision intentions, and the recoverability of historic loans to subsidiaries.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Debt Repayment (MRP) Judgements and Choices
findings.headline: Meridian Water debt repayment charges significantly higher than February 2026 budget, indicating project change or cost rise
findings.detail: Enfield's Q2 Treasury mid-year update will increase planned MRP charges for Meridian Water in 2027/28 from £1.4m to £3.2m. Over five years, this represents an additional £6.978m in planned debt service compared to the February 2026 budget. The increase reflects updated assumptions about when Meridian Water assets become available for intended use, suggesting either schedule delays or a revised project profile.
findings.matters: A material increase in debt service cash flow for a major capital project eight months into the year signals forecasting uncertainty and reduces financial flexibility, which concerns both lenders and the council's finance director.
findings.figures: £1.8m increase in 2027/28 (from £1.4m to £3.2m); £6.978m additional over five years
findings.quote: Q2 Treasury mid-year update will recommend increasing planned MRP charges for Meridian Water in 2027/28 from £1.4m to £3.2m, an increase of £1.8m.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Housing Gateway Ltd refocused on mitigating rent subsidy cap loss in homelessness temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The strategic review of Housing Gateway Ltd completed with revised business plan focusing on supporting council homelessness costs. Some temporary accommodation transferred to HGL to mitigate rent loss from the government subsidy cap. New acquisitions placed in HRA or General Fund instead of HGL to minimize SDLT.
findings.matters: Government subsidy cap on temporary accommodation is creating cost pressure in homelessness services. Council is restructuring HGL to manage this cost, indicating demand pressure that is not being reduced.
findings.figures: None quantified in this update
findings.quote: Its focus is on supporting the Council's costs of homelessness.  In this regard, the company offers an ability to mitigate the rent loss arising from the subsidy cap

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Capital receipts target of £50m set for 2026/27 to support debt reduction through asset disposal
findings.detail: The council has set a £50m capital receipts target for 2026/27 from disposals of surplus assets or assets where holding costs exceed income. This is part of asset rationalisation agenda with review scheduled for Q2.
findings.matters: Asset disposal is a finite, one-time source of cash. £50m target is substantial and time-dependent; slippage would impact the debt reduction strategy.
findings.figures: £50m target for 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has agreed a target of £50m capital receipts in 2026/27 which is being actively worked on through a pipeline of assets that have been deemed as surplus to requirements or where holding costs (revenue and capital) exceed income.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Energetik sale preferred option: Cabinet agreed in principle to full sale with Golden Share arrangement
findings.detail: The council is pursuing full sale of Energetik, a company holding £51.715m in council loans for energy projects. External advisors appointed; currently building data room and financial model prior to market testing. This is described as subject to outcome of market testing, engagement with lenders and due diligence completion.
findings.matters: Energetik represents embedded debt and operational complexity. The move toward sale signals the council recognizes this exposure needs to be removed or transferred; the 'subject to' conditions suggest risk this may not proceed.
findings.figures: £51.715m loans to Energetik
findings.quote: the preferred option is a full sale of Energetik supported by a Golden Share arrangement.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Finance team staffing crisis resolved: corporate accountancy reduced from 5 interim staff to 1 specialist through permanent appointments
findings.detail: At the start of 2025/26 the Director of Finance (Corporate) team had 5 interim members, now reduced to 1 specialist. New permanent appointments and a Trainee Accountant scheme introduced.
findings.matters: Reliance on 5 interim finance staff indicates the council faced capacity crisis in its financial management function. This matters for the quality of financial controls during a period of complex debt and restructuring decisions.
findings.figures: 5 interim staff reduced to 1 specialist
findings.quote: at the beginning of the financial year there were 5 interim members of staff in the corporate accountancy team which has now reduced to 1 specialist  due to the appointment of permanent staff.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Two schools unable to commit to repayment of licensed deficit arrangements despite council support
findings.detail: Following review of schools with rolling credit agreements, nine schools have submitted or are submitting licensed deficit agreements to the council. Two schools have advised they do not have sufficient budget to make repayments, requiring further negotiation on how deficits will be repaid.
findings.matters: Schools' deficits become the council's liability if not recovered; schools without repayment capacity indicate pressure in education demand or school funding.
findings.figures: 9 schools with agreements, 2 schools unable to afford repayment
findings.quote: Two schools have advised that they do not feel they have sufficient budget to make repayments and further work will be required to agree how these schools can repay the deficit balances.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: Risk reserves remain at minimum threshold of £43m with target of £83m forecast to be reached in three years
findings.detail: The council has only recently returned to the minimum reserve level and is building a recurring budget to rebuild reserves. The three-year timeline to reach target reserves indicates reserves were significantly depleted previously.
findings.matters: Below-target reserves indicate limited financial buffer for unexpected costs; three-year recovery period suggests the council experienced material financial stress.
findings.figures: £43m minimum threshold, £83m target, three-year timeline
findings.quote: Target Risk Reserves are forecast to be reached in three years.

findings.paper_title: 6 Month Review of the External Auditors Report
findings.headline: General Fund debt remains at £868m after reduction from £909m; Meridian Water sections being marketed to generate further capital receipts
findings.detail: External debt reduced by £41m during 2025/26. The council is pursuing capital receipts through marketing Meridian Water development sections to reduce the debt burden. However, £379.8m of the debt is the capital financing requirement for Meridian Water itself, which is embedded in the debt profile.
findings.matters: Debt levels of this magnitude directly constrain the council's borrowing capacity and debt servicing obligations. The reliance on development disposals to reduce debt is time-dependent and could slip.
findings.figures: £909m to £868m reduction, £379.8m Meridian Water capital financing requirement, £141.902m loans for house purchases, £51.715m subsidiary undertakings loans
findings.quote: External debt for the General Fund (including Meridian Water and Energetik) has reduced from £909m to £868m during 2025/26.

findings.headline: 9 audit actions from high and medium-risk findings remain overdue beyond implementation dates
findings.detail: Of 39 open audit actions as of 31 March 2026, 9 were not fully implemented by their original due dates (1 high-risk, 5 medium-risk, 3 low-risk). Delayed implementation of audit recommendations suggests slow management response to identified risks.
findings.matters: Overdue audit actions indicate either weak management accountability for implementing controls or resource constraints preventing timely remediation of identified weaknesses
findings.figures: 9 overdue actions out of 39 open actions; 1 high-risk, 5 medium-risk, 3 low-risk
findings.quote: Of these 9 actions (1 high risk, 5 medium risk and 3 low risk) were not fully implemented by their original due date, and are, therefore classed as overdue.

findings.headline: Schools collectively spending significant amounts on agency staffing without evidencing contract procedure rule compliance
findings.detail: Audit identified that schools are spending large amounts through staffing agencies but have not documented compliance with the council's contract procedure rules. This represents a specific control failure around procurement where spending is not fully justified or authorised.
findings.matters: Undocumented spending on agency staffing through multiple schools could hide cost overruns, suggest inefficient procurement practices, or indicate inadequate cost control in this high-value spending category
findings.figures: Multiple schools; amounts not quantified in report
findings.quote: Particular concerns were identified regarding agency staffing expenditure, with schools collectively spending significant amounts through agencies without fully evidencing compliance with the contract procedure rules.

findings.headline: High-risk audit findings increased to 7 in 2025-26 from zero in 2024-25
findings.detail: Schools identified 7 high-risk issues in 2025-26 compared to zero high-risk findings in the prior year. While no critical-risk findings were identified, the seven-fold increase in high-risk actions represents a concerning trend in emerging control failures.
findings.matters: Accelerating high-risk findings indicate growing weaknesses in school controls that require immediate management attention and could expose the council to financial or compliance risks
findings.figures: 7 high-risk actions in 2025-26; 0 high-risk actions in 2024-25; 70 total actions in 2025-26 vs 55 in 2024-25
findings.quote: Of the 70 actions agreed in 2025-26, none were critical risk and 7 were high risk. In 2024-25, 3 schools were audited all of which received a Reasonable assurance opinion. Of the 55 actions agreed in 2024-25, none were critical or high risk.

findings.headline: 50% of audited schools received limited assurance in 2025-26, down from 0% in 2024-25
findings.detail: Two of four schools audited received Limited assurance opinions in 2025-26, a deterioration from the prior year when three audited schools all received Reasonable assurance opinions. This represents a weakening trend in school governance and control across the sample.
findings.matters: Declining audit opinions in schools signal emerging control weaknesses that could affect the council's overall financial governance and its ability to manage school spending reliably
findings.figures: 2 schools Limited assurance, 2 Reasonable assurance in 2025-26; 3 schools Reasonable assurance in 2024-25; 0 schools Limited assurance in 2024-25
findings.quote: In 2025-26 full scope internal audits were carried out at 4 schools. 2 schools received a Reasonable assurance opinion and 2 received a Limited assurance opinion. In 2024-25, 3 schools were audited all of which received a Reasonable assurance opinion.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit team operating under sustained resource pressures: 3 audits deferred to 2026-27 due to recruitment difficulties
findings.detail: The Internal Audit team has not been able to fully recruit to its approved structure. This resulted in deferral of 3 internal audits from the 2025-26 plan. However, the Head of Internal Audit states available resources were 'sufficient to fulfil Internal Audit's mandate' — though this constrains breadth of assurance coverage.
findings.matters: Sustained resource constraints on internal audit reduce the council's ability to comprehensively assess control effectiveness. This is a structural vulnerability that persists and limits forward assurance capability.
findings.figures: 3 audits deferred; recruitment to approved structure not achieved
findings.quote: Changes included the deferral of 3 internal audits to 2026-27 due to resource pressures in the Internal Audit team. The resource issues were difficulties in recruiting to the approved structure

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Cyber security risk management framework incomplete and inconsistently embedded; no formally documented cybersecurity strategy
findings.detail: High-risk audit finding on cyber security identified that the Council lacks a fully defined cybersecurity risk management approach with limited enterprise-wide visibility. Council has a Digital, Data and AI Strategy but this is not supported by a dedicated cybersecurity strategy. Legacy platforms continue without consolidated migration timeline.
findings.matters: Incomplete cyber governance and lack of formal strategy increases risk of data breach, service disruption, or financial system compromise — all of material concern to lenders evaluating council operational resilience.
findings.figures: High-risk finding; legacy platforms without consolidated migration timeline
findings.quote: The Council lacks a fully defined and consistently embedded cybersecurity risk management approach, resulting in limited enterprise-wide visibility, inconsistent assessment and escalation, unclear accountability, and reduced assurance over the management of cyber risks and threats

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit function itself only 'partially conforms' with professional standards; external quality assessment identified gaps
findings.detail: External Quality Assessment by Chartered Institute of Internal Auditors found Enfield Council's internal audit function 'partially conforms' with Public Sector Internal Audit Standards. Internal assessment for 2025-26 confirms opinion remains at 'partially conforms'. Quality assurance improvement programme still in progress with multiple actions not yet started.
findings.matters: If internal audit — the council's primary control assurance mechanism — is itself only partially conforming with standards, confidence in the council's ability to identify and manage risks is materially reduced. This undermines the reliability of control assessments across the organisation.
findings.figures: 1 out of 5 years assessment complete (External Quality Assessment in Jan 2025); 'partially conforms' finding
findings.quote: The overall assessment was that Enfield Council's Internal Audit function partially conforms to the Public Sector Internal Audit Standards... whilst progress has been made in implementing the QAIP, the Head of Internal Audit's opinion remains at partially conforms

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council-owned Energetik company has incomplete governance, no shareholder framework, and unmanaged conflict-of-interest between council's dual role as shareholder and lender
findings.detail: Limited assurance audit of Energetik (the council's energy company) found governance documentation incomplete and outdated. Articles of Association not reviewed since 2019 despite three-yearly requirement. No Council-wide shareholder governance framework was in place during the audit period. No protocol exists for the structural conflict arising from the council's dual role as sole shareholder and sole lender.
findings.matters: A council's ability to govern and monitor subsidiary companies is material to overall financial risk. Unmanaged conflicts of interest and absent governance frameworks are red flags for arm's-length bodies and suggest broader governance control gaps.
findings.figures: Energetik: Limited assurance opinion; governance review gap since 2019
findings.quote: No conflict of interest management provisions across Energetik governance forums; no protocol for the inherent shareholder/lender conflict. Council-wide frameworks address personal conflicts but the structural conflict arising from the Council's dual role as sole shareholder and sole lender has not been formally assessed, documented, or managed

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: SEN audit identified 'No assurance' — safeguarding checks completed after services commenced for one supplier
findings.detail: The audit of SEN Procurement and Payments identified weaknesses in due diligence where safeguarding and due diligence checks for one supplier were completed only after services had commenced. This exposes vulnerable service users and creates reputational risk.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating council governance needs to see effective safeguarding controls, particularly for vulnerable populations. Post-service commencement checks suggest breakdown in control design and risk management discipline.
findings.figures: 1 supplier case identified
findings.quote: the audit identified that due diligence and safeguarding checks for one supplier were completed only after services had commenced, increasing the risk that vulnerable service users may be exposed to providers before required checks have been completed

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Grant Thornton statutory recommendation on debt and reserves: council must 'prioritise debt reduction and lower debt servicing costs, while rebuilding risk reserves to the £43m minimum threshold and moving towards the £83m target'
findings.detail: External auditors have issued a formal statutory recommendation requiring the council to reduce its debt burden and rebuild reserves. The current position is below the £43m minimum threshold that auditors deem necessary. Positive management action has been taken but this is an explicit pressure point.
findings.matters: A statutory recommendation on debt and reserves is a material governance issue. PWLB lenders rely on council reserve adequacy; a council below its own minimum threshold presents elevated risk and suggests borrowing may be constrained or costly.
findings.figures: £43m minimum reserve threshold; £83m target threshold
findings.quote: Grant Thornton issued a statutory recommendation where it was advised that the Council should prioritise debt reduction and lower debt servicing costs, while rebuilding risk reserves to the £43m minimum threshold and moving towards the £83m target through recurring savings

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit and Counter Fraud Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £8.1m of SEN spending (26% of third-party payments) processed through AP1 workaround payments rather than standard controls
findings.detail: SEN procurement does not comply with Contract Procedure Rules. Despite a July 2025 request from Strategic Finance to limit AP1 payments, £5.5m (67% of AP1 payments) continued to be processed this way between August 2025 and March 2026. The service cannot confirm the total number or value of overdue and unpaid invoices.
findings.matters: This indicates loss of control over a material area of spend (26% of SEN third-party payments), weak financial governance, and inability to track actual liabilities - directly affecting accuracy of council financial reporting and risk to lenders evaluating council financial discipline.
findings.figures: £8.1m processed via AP1 in 2025-26; £5.5m via AP1 between August 2025 and March 2026 despite directive to limit use
findings.quote: In 2025–26, £8.1m of SEN expenditure, representing 26% of total SEN third party payments, was processed through AP1 payments rather than the Council's standard Neptune payment process

findings.headline: Prior-year audit assurance issues require resolution before opinions can be issued.
findings.detail: The report notes a 'regaining assurance process' for prior years' accounts balances. This process is described as necessary to 'allow audit opinions to be issued in future years', implying prior-year opinions were qualified or withheld due to unresolved audit concerns. The document does not detail what the underlying issues were.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit issues on prior-year accounts suggest potential control weaknesses or accounting problems; lenders need to know if there are ongoing audit concerns or material adjustments pending.
findings.figures: None provided in the document body.
findings.quote: The report also includes wider audit updates including the process for regaining assurance for the audit of prior years' accounts balances which would allow audit opinions to be issued in future years.

findings.headline: Debt servicing ratio has limited headroom above affordability ceiling
findings.detail: General Fund debt servicing costs are 7.5% of net revenue budget, comfortably within the 10-12% target range. However, if IFRS 16 lease accounting impacts are included (mainly relating to temporary accommodation), the ratio would rise to 12.3%, breaching the upper affordability limit. The council treats this as 'presentational only' but it leaves no margin for cash pressures.
findings.matters: A debt servicing ratio at the ceiling would materially constrain the council's financial flexibility and ability to respond to unforeseen demands or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: Actual 7.5% NRB; with IFRS 16 treatment would be 12.3% (above 10-12% range)
findings.quote: The affordability indicator expressed by reference to Net Revenue Budget (NRB) is 7.5% which is within the 10-12% target range.

findings.headline: HRA refinancing risk elevated as proportion of fixed-rate debt declines
findings.detail: Although overall refinancing risk is low and within approved limits, the HRA is exposed to higher refinancing risk because a declining proportion of its financing requirement is fixed-rate. The council uses variable-rate repayment loans to spread interest rate risk, leaving future refinancing vulnerable to rate movements. HRA Interest Cover Ratio is 1.85x against a minimum target of 1.25x, and LTV at 51% is at the 50% maximum.
findings.matters: This represents material tail risk to HRA affordability if interest rates remain elevated; higher future refinancing rates could breach affordability ratios.
findings.figures: HRA ICR 1.85x (target 1.25x minimum); LTV 51% (target 50% maximum)
findings.quote: The refinancing risk for the HRA is higher because over time, a lower proportion of the financing requirement is already fixed with existing loans.

findings.headline: Energetik lending continues with £8.7m new advances during the year
findings.detail: The council extended £8.7m in loans to Energetik during 2025/26, of which £565k was grant-funded and converted to equity. Additionally, a £3.0m rebalancing of Energetik's Tranche 1 funding was reclassified from revenue to capital. Total subsidiary exposure now stands at £220.8m (HGL £146.1m, Energetik £74.7m).
findings.matters: Continued lending to Energetik increases subsidiary exposure at a time when the council has already provisioned for £15.591m credit loss risk, signalling the lender has concerns about the entity's sustainability.
findings.figures: £8.7m advanced (£565k grant-supported); Energetik total exposure £74.7m; total subsidiary exposure £220.8m
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council extended £8.7m loans to Energetik of which £565k was supported by external grant and converted into an equity investment.

findings.headline: Subsidiary loan portfolio carries £25.3m in unrecognized credit losses
findings.detail: Mandatory Expected Credit Loss (ECL) provisions require the council to recognize potential loan losses on its subsidiaries: HGL faces estimated risk of £9.693m and Energetik £15.591m. These are being charged to reserves over time (HGL as one-off, Energetik over 25 years). In 2025/26 alone, £494k was charged, with Energetik's charge including £106k of voluntary provision reflecting lower interest rates on its loans.
findings.matters: These contingent liabilities represent real credit risk in the council's loan book; they reduce useable reserves and constrain financial flexibility.
findings.figures: HGL £9.693m risk (£98k charged), Energetik £15.591m risk (£396k charged in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Estimated risk to loans (to be provided for over time): HGL £9,693k, Energetik £15,591k. Charges to be applied over time horizon: HGL One off, Energetik 25 yrs.

findings.headline: School deficits growing with recovery plans still to be agreed
findings.detail: Schools owed the council £6.9m as at 31 March 2026, up from £6.4m the prior year. Twelve schools are in deficit, but four of these have repayment plans that are still to be agreed with the council. The licensed deficit arrangement uses council reserves to lend to schools, which directly reduces internal borrowing capacity and forces additional external borrowing.
findings.matters: Growing school deficits with uncertain recovery timelines indicate cash management pressure and governance risk; they also increase the council's debt servicing requirement.
findings.figures: £6.9m (2024/25 £6.4m); twelve schools affected; four with repayment plans to be agreed
findings.quote: The £6.9m debt outstanding as at 31st March 2026 relates to twelve schools, four of which have repayment plans to be agreed with the Council.

findings.headline: Planned savings delivery fell short by £3.9m, with £2.9m deferred to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council planned £20.1m of savings for 2025/26 but delivered only £16.3m. £2.9m are deferred to 2026/27 and £1.0m are being redesigned. This shortfall suggests implementation challenges with efficiency programmes at a time when the council is already overspending and relying on exceptional government support.
findings.matters: Savings slippage means planned budget reductions are not materialising; combined with existing demand pressures, this signals difficulty translating plans into cash reductions
findings.figures: £16.3m delivered of £20.1m planned savings (£3.9m shortfall); £2.9m deferred to 2026/27; £1.0m being redesigned
findings.quote: Out of £20.1m planned savings for 2025/26, £16.3m were delivered, with £2.9m to be delivered next year and savings of £1.0m are being redesigned. This means that there was a shortfall in-year of £3.9m.

findings.headline: Risk reserves recovered to only £46.1m, exceeding the £43.3m minimum threshold by just £2.8m
findings.detail: Risk reserves have been rebuilt from historical lows caused by £21m overspend in 2022/23 and £39m in 2023/24. They now stand at £46.1m, which just exceeds the council's minimum threshold of £43.3m by £2.8m. The recovery relied partly on exceptional financial support (applying capital receipts to revenue) as a one-off measure, rather than structural budget improvement.
findings.matters: A £2.8m buffer on minimum reserves is a thin cushion for a council facing ongoing demand pressures in social care and education; limited headroom constrains ability to absorb shocks
findings.figures: Risk reserves £46.1m at year-end; minimum threshold £43.3m; buffer £2.8m; opening balance £32.4m
findings.quote: Risk reserves remain a key area of focus to improve the council's financial resilience. During the year, risk reserves increased from £32.4m to £46.3m. This means that Risk Reserves achieved the minimum reserve levels that the council judged to be required (£43.3m) by the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reached £20.8m with government reimbursement conditional on SEND reform delivery
findings.detail: The DSG ended 2025/26 with a £3.4m in-year overspend, bringing the cumulative deficit to £20.8m. This is driven by SEND placements and costs. While the government has committed to reimbursing 90% of the deficit as a grant (£18.7m), this funding is conditional on the council meeting local SEND reform plan conditions. The council is currently bearing £0.9m per annum interest cost on the deficit.
findings.matters: A £20.8m cumulative deficit in a ring-fenced grant represents a structural unfunded liability; conditional reimbursement introduces execution risk if SEND reform targets are not met
findings.figures: £20.8m cumulative DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026; £3.4m in-year overspend; £0.9m annual interest cost
findings.quote: £3.4m in-year overspend resulting in a £20.8m deficit. The government has confirmed that, subject to local SEND reform plan conditions being met, 90% of the DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026 will be provided to the council as a grant.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation lease programme acquired only 312 properties against planned 800, underspending £127m of capital budget
findings.detail: The council's strategy to manage homelessness through long-lease property acquisition acquired only 312 properties in 2025/26 against a planned 800 (39% of target). The £189.8m capital budget underspent by £127m. The council attributes this to challenging market conditions including high property prices and competition from institutional investors. While the paper expects market conditions to improve, the strategy has not delivered at planned scale.
findings.matters: A £127m underspend on a £189.8m budget represents a major capital programme failure for a key council strategy; homelessness demand continues to grow and the council's mitigation strategy is not scaling
findings.figures: 312 properties acquired vs 800 planned; temporary accommodation budget £189.8m, actual spend £62.8m (55% delivery)
findings.quote: The original budget assumed the acquisition of 800 long-lease properties during the year; however, only 312 were secured. Despite the ongoing efforts of the team, this shortfall reflects challenging market conditions, which have limited the ability to deliver the Lease+ programme at scale.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £15.1m due to structural growth in demand for older residents and complex needs support
findings.detail: Adult Social Care experienced a £15.1m overspend against budget, representing the largest driver of the council's overall £6.4m general fund overspend. The council required £10m in exceptional financial support (from capital receipts) to prevent this from consuming reserves. The paper identifies this as a structural issue: more older residents and adults with complex needs are requiring support, particularly following hospital discharge, a national trend affecting all local authorities.
findings.matters: A £15m social care overspend on a £124m base is material; it is explicitly identified as structural demand growth rather than one-off costs, suggesting ongoing budget pressures ahead
findings.figures: Adult Social Care net expenditure £124m; overspend £15.1m; £10m exceptional financial support applied
findings.quote: More older residents and adults with complex needs required support, particularly following hospital discharge. This is a national issue affecting all local authorities. The council continues to work to support people safely at home where possible, improve local provision and control costs without reducing care.

findings.paper_title: 4. Appendix A - 2025 Valuation - Final Results Report (London Borough of Enfield Pension Fund)
findings.headline: Fund's assumptions significantly more optimistic than standardised benchmarks
findings.detail: The fund reports a 127% funding level on its own assumptions but only 106% on the Standardised Assumptions Basis used for comparison across LGPS funds. This 21-point gap reflects the fund's higher discount rate assumption (5.9% vs a lower standard) and suggests the improvement is partly driven by assumption changes rather than asset gains.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand whether improved funding is real (asset growth) or assumption-driven (which can reverse). The gap signals the fund's position is partly dependent on market assumptions holding
findings.figures: Funding level 127% on fund basis vs 106% on SAB basis
findings.quote: The Fund's SAB funding level at 31 March 2025 is 106%. SAB assumptions are to allow comparison only and are not intended to be appropriate for funding or setting contribution rates.

findings.paper_title: 4. Appendix A - 2025 Valuation - Final Results Report (London Borough of Enfield Pension Fund)
findings.headline: Recent experience worse than assumptions; investment returns underperformed and inflation spiked
findings.detail: Between the 2022 and 2025 valuations, actual investment returns were 1.6% p.a. versus the 4.4% assumed (£138m shortfall), and inflation ran at 6.1% versus the 2.3% assumed (£187m cost). Yet the valuation improved the funding position because investment outlook assumptions were raised going forward. This reliance on future returns that have not yet materialized is a risk.
findings.matters: If investment returns and inflation continue to diverge from the 5.9% p.a. assumed for this valuation, the council could face contribution increases at the 2028 revaluation, squeezing future budgets
findings.figures: Investment returns 1.6% actual vs 4.4% expected (impact -£138m), benefit inflation 6.1% actual vs 2.3% expected (impact -£187m), salary inflation 6.2% actual vs 4.2% expected (impact -£12m)
findings.quote: The funding position, and the Fund's funding strategy, are sensitive to various sources of risks. These funding risks broadly fall into categories of economic, demographic, regulatory and other.

findings.paper_title: 4. Appendix A - 2025 Valuation - Final Results Report (London Borough of Enfield Pension Fund)
findings.headline: Employer contribution rates reduced; the council pays less into the pension fund
findings.detail: The council's combined contribution rate falls from 18.9% to 16.0% of payroll over 2026/27-2028/29, with secondary rates negative (meaning the council receives a payment adjustment of -1.8% per year). This frees up circa £4.8m annually at current payroll. Contributions are stable at a floor of 16% for the three-year period.
findings.matters: Pensions are the council's largest controllable cost after payroll. A reduction of 2.9% of payroll means material budget space for services or reserves
findings.figures: Primary rate 17.8% (down from 18.9%), secondary rate -1.8% annually (down from 0%), total rate 16.0%
findings.quote: On average, employer total contribution rates (ie Primary plus Secondary) have reduced mainly due to higher assumed future investment returns at 2025 compared to 2022.

findings.paper_title: KD5993 - Rent Setting Report 2026-27 Full Council
findings.headline: HRA reserves are falling to the minimum threshold, leaving almost no buffer for emergencies or service shocks.
findings.detail: The estimated HRA balance at 1 April 2026 is £9.3m, down from £15.9m at 1 April 2025. The minimum requirement is £8m–£15m. This is planned use to fund the capital programme, but the council is now operating at the lower end of its prudent range with minimal headroom for unexpected costs or income volatility.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council has financial buffers to manage emergencies (e.g., building failures, compliance costs, rent arrears) without triggering further borrowing.
findings.figures: HRA balance: £15.9m (2025) declining to £9.3m (2026); minimum requirement £8–£15m
findings.quote: The estimated remaining level is within the HRA's minimum requirement of 10% of turnover £9.57m.

findings.paper_title: KD5993 - Rent Setting Report 2026-27 Full Council
findings.headline: HRA concessionary borrowing rates (0.4% discount) expire June 2026 with no confirmation yet that they will continue.
findings.detail: The business plan assumes borrowing at an average of 5% from 2026-27 onwards, which includes the concessionary rate. If the 0.4% discount ends (as it may), the average rate would rise to approximately 5.4%. The paper notes an update is expected in January 2026 but this is a material risk that remains unresolved.
findings.matters: A jump in interest costs would immediately worsen affordability metrics and reduce the council's debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Assumed borrowing rate 5% including concessionary rate; current average 4.9% for 2025-26
findings.quote: We are expecting an update in January 2026 to confirm whether HRA concessionary rates will continue past March 2026.

findings.paper_title: KD5993 - Rent Setting Report 2026-27 Full Council
findings.headline: Efficiency savings of £1m per annum are unproven and critical to maintaining prudential borrowing ratios.
findings.detail: The Interest Cover Ratio of 1.85 sits above the 1.25 minimum, but the paper explicitly states this depends on achieving the proposed £1m annual savings. The savings are described as being "partly achieved by" three initiatives (better housing management systems, technology in repairs, tenant behaviour campaigns) but no detailed costing or proof of achievability is provided. If these savings don't materialize, the ratio could fall below the minimum threshold.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's key financial metric depends on speculative savings or proven efficiency.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio 1.85 vs minimum 1.25; efficiency savings £1m per annum until 2028-29
findings.quote: It should be noted that remaining above the recommended level is dependent on the revenue budget achieving the proposed savings as set out in the revenue section of this report.

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: One-off asset sales being used to fund capital spend with no sustainability beyond this decade
findings.detail: The use of capital receipts at the assumed scale (£110.4 million over 10 years, mostly in the first 5 years) is described as a 'one-off' measure. The council is unlikely to have the same scale of disposable assets in future years. This means the current affordability metric is not sustainable beyond the 10-year programme horizon.
findings.matters: A lender should note that the council is using a one-time source to fund ongoing capital commitments. The post-2035 position is likely to be materially tighter, with CFR growing again once large asset disposals are depleted.
findings.figures: £110.4 million future capital receipts assumed; £97.6 million to replace in-year borrowing; £12.8 million to reduce historic borrowing
findings.quote: The use of capital receipts at this scale is a 'one-off' measure. The Council is unlikely to have the same scale of disposable assets to fund capital spend in future years.

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: £82.4 million unspent budget carried forward from 2025/26 signals execution challenges
findings.detail: The council has carried forward £82.4 million in unspent capital budget from 2025/26 into 2026/27. This consists of £10.5 million approved by Cabinet in June 2025 and £71.9 million unspent forecast at Quarter 3 (including £40 million for HRA). Large carryforwards suggest the council either overestimated its spending capacity or encountered delivery delays.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director would want to understand why the planned spend did not materialise. This raises questions about project readiness, procurement, or capacity. If the council cannot deliver a planned capital programme, it raises concerns about its ability to manage and execute the ambitious 10-year plan.
findings.figures: £82.4 million carried forward from 2025/26; £40 million HRA element
findings.quote: £82.4 million unspent budget proposed to be carried forward from 2025/26 into 2026/27. This consists of £10.5 million approved by Cabinet in June 2025 (Quarter 1) (KD 5900) and £71.9 million unspent budget forecast at Quarter 3, including £40.0 million for the HRA

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: £549.7 million temporary accommodation programme is a capital solution to a revenue budget pressure, dependent on high occupancy rates
findings.detail: The council is acquiring 657 homes over three years (£549.7 million capital spend) to provide temporary accommodation for residents. This is explicitly to 'alleviate revenue budget housing pressures'. The financial case depends on careful management of unit location and achieving forecast tenant occupancy rates to realise savings in housing revenue budgets. If occupancy rates fall short, these savings will not materialize.
findings.matters: This is a material transfer of problem from revenue to capital. The council is using £549.7 million of capital (which typically requires borrowing) to solve what is fundamentally a housing affordability and demand problem on the revenue side. If the temporary accommodation assets underperform, the council has capital and debt with weak asset backing.
findings.figures: £549.7 million 10-year temporary accommodation budget; £185.3 million in 2026/27 alone; 657 homes in leases over 3 years; upfront 'accounting value' with cash spread over lease life
findings.quote: The location of these new accommodation units will be carefully managed, to ensure a good level of tenant occupancy, to ensure forecast savings in housing revenue budgets are realised.

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: Major grant and s106 contributions have not yet been secured or cash received
findings.detail: The 10-year capital programme includes ambitious place-shaping plans (sustainable transport, flood management, town centre improvements) that rely on significant capital grant funding, s106 contributions, and Community Infrastructure Levy receipts. The majority of this funding has not been secured or cash received. If external funding is not available, the programme will have to be managed within existing approved resources and future spend restricted.
findings.matters: This is a second major dependency risk: not only is the council dependent on asset sales, but it is also dependent on receipt of external grants and s106 contributions that have not been committed. Inability to collect these would force programme cuts.
findings.figures: £483.5 million in grants assumed over 10 years; £8.5 million s106/CIL; the majority not yet secured or cash received
findings.quote: These plans rely on significant levels of capital grant, s106 contributions and Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL), the majority of which has not yet been secured or cash received. The 10-year programme will have to be managed from within existing approved resources and future planned spend restricted if external funding is not available.

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: Meridian Water regeneration faces rising construction costs, delivery delays, and uncertainty over commercial partners
findings.detail: Meridian Water's £170.3 million 10-year capital programme is at risk from multiple delivery factors. The council has removed £71.1 million of borrowing from earlier plans but is now assuming £49.2 million growth for additional infrastructure. Capitalised interest costs have increased by £12.9 million due to slower, lower-value receipts arriving later than originally assumed.
findings.matters: Meridian Water is a major long-term commitment with substantial debt implications. Delays or cost inflation would directly pressure the council's borrowing position and capital programme. A lender would want to know the commercial case and exit strategies.
findings.figures: £170.3 million 10-year Meridian Water spend; £71.1 million borrowing removed; £49.2 million infrastructure growth added; £12.9 million additional capitalised interest
findings.quote: Given the current challenging investment climate in the UK construction industry, Meridian Water faces rising construction costs, infrastructure and delivery delays, funding uncertainties, and challenges securing long-term commercial and residential partners.

findings.paper_title: REVISED Appendix B Capital Programme 2026-27 to 2035-36 Council
findings.headline: £130 million of the affordability case depends on asset sales that have not yet been received
findings.detail: The council is using a new affordability target to keep the capital financing requirement (CFR) below £997 million (the 2024/25 closing position). This target can only be met if at least £130 million in capital receipts from asset disposals are generated within the first 5 years. If these receipts are not achieved, the council will have to curtail spending or find alternative funding, and CFR will exceed the affordability target.
findings.matters: This is a material single-point-of-failure in the council's financial plan. A lender would be concerned that the council's affordability story depends entirely on asset sales that have not yet happened, and that there is no credible fallback.
findings.figures: £130 million target receipts; £997 million CFR ceiling; £110.4 million already assumed for core services capital spend
findings.quote: There is risk over the value and timing of these future receipts. If receipts are not achieved to the extent currently assumed, capital spend will either have to be curtailed or alternative non-borrowing funding sources identified to meet affordability metric.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27 Cover Report- Council Final
findings.headline: The council is targeting £130m of capital receipts over 5 years, with £42.6m in 2026/27 earmarked for debt reduction
findings.detail: Rather than fund all capital investment with new borrowing, the council has set a capital receipts disposal target of £130m over 2026/27-2030/31. Of the £50m receipts target for 2026/27, £42.6m will be used to reduce historic borrowing (generating approximately £700k annual interest saving) and £9.4m for transformational revenue spending. This strategy is core to the council's affordability plan.
findings.matters: This strategy constrains new borrowing, which is prudent. However, it creates dependency on actually generating the forecasted receipts—if receipts underperform, the council faces either delayed debt reduction or deferred capital projects.
findings.figures: £130m receipts target over 5 years; £50m in 2026/27; £42.6m for debt repayment; approximately £700k annual interest saving
findings.quote: The capital receipts disposals target for the next 5 years is £130m, with a target of £50m set for 2026/27, of which £42.6m is earmarked for funding the in-year capital programme and debt repayment resulting in revenue budget saving of  circa £700k

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27 Cover Report- Council Final
findings.headline: The council faces substantial revenue budget pressures that may limit capital delivery even in approved projects
findings.detail: The document identifies 'substantial revenue budget pressures' as a key risk and warns that 'ongoing budget constraints and the need to maintain financial sustainability may limit the Council's ability to deliver projects requiring significant amounts of borrowing.' While debt financing costs remain below the 10-12% target, there is an acknowledged risk that capital programme costs may exceed current forecasts.
findings.matters: This signals the council's revenue budget is under independent strain. If revenues deteriorate, the council may need to defer or scale back even capital projects already approved, creating delivery risk.
findings.figures: Target debt financing: 10-12% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: the Council faces substantial revenue budget pressures. There is a risk that the revenue cost of the capital programme is higher than that detailed in the TMSS.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27 Cover Report- Council Final
findings.headline: Meridian Water, a key source of assumed capital receipts for debt reduction, faces substantial delivery and commercial risks
findings.detail: The 10-year capital programme's long-term affordability depends on significant capital receipts from Meridian Water land parcels. However, the document explicitly flags that the programme 'continues to face substantial risks due to sector‑wide construction cost inflation, delays in infrastructure and scheme delivery, funding uncertainties, and challenges in securing long‑ term commercial and residential development partners.'
findings.matters: Meridian Water is critical to the council's receipts strategy for debt reduction. If the project underperforms, the council loses expected cash inflows, forcing either debt reduction plans to be abandoned or other capital projects to be cut.
findings.figures: £56.2m allocated for Meridian Water in 2026/27 (£42.5m grant funded); £170.3m over 10 years
findings.quote: the programme continues to face substantial risks due to sector‑wide construction cost inflation, delays in infrastructure and scheme delivery, funding uncertainties, and challenges in securing long‑ term commercial and residential development partners.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy and Capital Programme 2026-27 Cover Report- Council Final
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation is £185.3m of the 2026/27 General Fund capital budget, representing 55% of General Fund capital spend
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 capital budget includes £185.3m for temporary accommodation solutions, with additional commitments of £214.9m in 2027/28 and £149.5m in 2028/29, totalling £549.7m over three years. This is financed through 'other credit arrangements' (revenue budgets that fund leases) rather than capital receipts or borrowing, indicating lease-based acquisition rather than asset ownership.
findings.matters: This massive capital commitment signals substantial housing pressure requiring ongoing revenue funding for lease payments. For a lender, it indicates a housing crisis consuming significant resources; for the finance director, it's a major revenue budget headwind for years.
findings.quote: Approves a Capital budget for 2026/27 of £476.4m (General Fund £334.1m including £185.3m temporary accommodation solutions & HRA £142.1m).

findings.headline: Edmonton Leisure Centre investment projected to result in £0.4m loss
findings.detail: The council invested £2.5m in Edmonton Leisure Centre refurbishment but expects to receive only £2.1m back over 30 years. The difference is explicitly treated as a loss to support the partner's VAT position, charged to the General Fund.
findings.matters: An explicit acceptance that a service investment will not achieve full recovery, signalling either overpayment or deteriorated circumstances.
findings.figures: £2.5m invested; £2.1m expected repayment; £0.4m loss allowance
findings.quote: The Council invested £2.5m to support refurbishment of the Leisure Centre and is expecting repayment of £2.1m over 30 years, with the balance £0.4m payable to HM Revenue & Customs to safeguard GLL's VAT position which forms part of the agreement. The ECL of £0.4m acknowledges the shortfall in eventual loan repayments as a charge to the Council's General Fund.

findings.headline: Energetik infrastructure is illiquid; recovery would be complex in default
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that Energetik's assets — energy infrastructure — cannot be quickly converted to cash. The council's mitigation relies entirely on Energetik remaining solvent and able to service interest and principal, with no collateral swap-out available.
findings.matters: In a stress scenario, the council cannot liquidate Energetik's infrastructure to recover its £69.5m investment, leaving it exposed if the company fails.
findings.figures: £69.5m invested in Energetik with illiquid infrastructure backing
findings.quote: Energetik presents higher risks to the Council as lender because Energetik is building infrastructure, which is not a 'liquid' asset. i.e. a sale would be complex.

findings.headline: Service investments producing zero income and none forecast for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's two major service investments — HGL (£141.9m loans) and Energetik (£69.5m invested) — generated no income in 2025/26 and none is forecast for the year ahead. These represent cost centres to the council, not revenue generators.
findings.matters: Large borrowings to fund non-income-generating investments increase the council's reliance on other revenue streams; any revenue pressure cannot be offset by these investments.
findings.figures: HGL and Energetik income: £0m in 2025/26 and £0m forecast for 2026/27
