findings.quote: The Council's Service investments in Energetik and HGL have generated no income in 2025/26 and none is forecast for 2026/27 therefore there is nothing to report on this indicator.

findings.headline: Energetik carries substantial loss allowance relative to loan book, signalling credit concerns
findings.detail: The council has set aside £30.4m expected credit loss (loss allowance) against £51.7m in Energetik loans — a 59% write-down. While the council states it does not expect actual losses, the accounting adjustment reflects statistical likelihood of non-payment. HGL loans carry zero loss allowance by comparison.
findings.matters: High loss allowance indicates the council itself has doubts about Energetik's ability to service the debt, independent of the strategic review.
findings.figures: Energetik loans £51.7m; loss allowance £30.4m (59% of nominal); HGL loans £141.9m with £0 loss allowance
findings.quote: Energetik – total loans 51.7 [£m, with] Loss allowance -30.4

findings.headline: Strategic review of Energetik underway amid Meridian Water changes
findings.detail: Energetik, in which the council has invested £69.5m (£51.7m loans plus £17.8m equity), is undergoing formal strategic review. The review is specifically framed as identifying and mitigating risks in the context of wider changes to Meridian Water scheme, the larger development on which Energetik depends.
findings.matters: A strategic reassessment of a £70m investment signals the council has identified material risks that need mitigation; lenders need to understand what those risks are.
findings.figures: £69.5m total invested in Energetik as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: A strategic review of Energetik is being undertaken to identify and mitigate risks to the Council in the context of wider changes to the Meridian Water scheme.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting mandatory from April 2024 increases recorded liabilities and impacts capital financing metrics
findings.detail: The Council has reclassified all lease obligations under IFRS 16 accounting rules (mandatory from April 2024), moving leases from off-balance-sheet operating leases to on-balance-sheet Right-of-Use assets with corresponding liabilities. This increases reported assets and liabilities and impacts the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR).
findings.matters: As the Council shifts temporary accommodation funding toward leases, IFRS 16 treatment will increase recorded liabilities and affect capital financing affordability metrics used to assess financial sustainability
findings.figures: IFRS 16 mandatory from 1 April 2024; all lease liabilities reclassified from that date
findings.quote: IFRS 16 became mandatory for the Council from April 2024, and all lease liabilities have been classified and accounted for in accordance with this standard from that date.

findings.headline: General Fund debt held at £997m with new ceiling target set to prevent further growth
findings.detail: The Council has adopted a target to keep General Fund debt below £997m (excluding projects with direct revenue savings), which was the actual debt level in 2024/25. This represents an explicit cap on future borrowing.
findings.matters: An explicit debt ceiling at current levels signals the Council considers its borrowing unsustainable and is unable to absorb further debt growth, limiting capacity for additional capital investment or borrowing flexibility
findings.figures: General Fund debt £997m in 2024/25; ceiling target set at this level
findings.quote: Adopting an additional target of keeping the General Fund debt below £997m (excluding any new projects with direct revenue savings). £997m was the General Fund debt in 2024/25 including internal and external borrowing.

findings.headline: £42.9m of capital receipts assumed as critical funding source for 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme relies on an assumption that £42.9m in capital receipts will be generated and deployed to fund the programme. This is stated as essential to facilitating reduction of overall Council debt in the medium term.
findings.matters: If capital receipts are not realised as planned, there is an immediate funding gap that would require alternative financing, programme cuts, or increased borrowing
findings.figures: £42.9m capital receipts assumed for 2026/27; integral to debt reduction strategy
findings.quote: The 2026/27 capital budget assumes £42.9m of capital receipts will be used to fund the capital programme. This, in addition to ongoing work to maximise external grants, will facilitate the reduction of overall Council debt in the medium term.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand identified as key operational and financial challenge driving capital strategy
findings.detail: The Council explicitly flags increased demand for temporary accommodation as a significant challenge. In response, it is exploring long-term leases for properties rather than outright purchase as an alternative funding approach.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand can create budget volatility and unfunded pressures; shifting strategy from purchase to leasing changes the capital financing profile and triggers IFRS 16 lease accounting treatment
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation presented as primary operational and financial challenge requiring strategic response
findings.quote: One key operational and financial challenge for the Council is the increased demand for temporary accommodation. In response, the Council continues to explore a wide range of options, including entering into long-term leases for appropriate properties as an alternative to outright purchase.

findings.headline: Government creation of new employment negotiating bodies for school and care staff with funding unclear from 2027/28
findings.detail: The Employment Rights Bill will establish a School Support Staff Negotiating Body (starting 2027/28) and an Adult Social Care Negotiating Body (starting 2028) outside current national agreements. The document notes it 'remains unclear whether pay and other terms from these bodies will be fully funded or how any unfunded costs may affect councils'.
findings.matters: These bodies will set pay for two large budget areas; unknown costs are a material budget risk in the MTFP period
findings.figures: Effective dates: 2027/28 (school staff), 2028 (care staff)
findings.quote: The Government plans to establish two new negotiating bodies - the School Support Staff Negotiating Body (SSSNB) for non-teaching school staff and the Adult Social Care Negotiating Body (ASCNB) for adult social care workers - through the Employment Rights Bill introduced on 10 October 2024. These bodies, which fall outside current national agreements (NJC and JNC), are set to begin in the 2027/28 academic year (SSSNB) and in 2028 (ASCNB). It remains unclear whether pay and other terms from these bodies will be fully funded or how any unfunded costs may affect councils and providers.

findings.headline: Council Tax increased 4.99%, the maximum allowable before a referendum becomes required
findings.detail: The council is increasing Council Tax by the full threshold of 4.99% (2.99% core plus 2.00% Adult Social Care precept) before a referendum becomes necessary. This represents £1.60 per week for a Band D property and signals the council is maximizing tax revenue to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Maximizing tax at the referendum threshold leaves no room for further income growth without a costly public vote
findings.figures: 4.99% increase; 2.99% core plus 2.00% Adult Social Care precept; £1.60 per week increase for Band D
findings.quote: Note that the Band D property rate in 2026/27 for Enfield will be £1,757.16. This includes a 2.99% general Council Tax increase and a 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept and represents an increase of £1.60 per week.

findings.headline: Savings deliverability adjustment added for first time to budget to cover optimism bias and slippage
findings.detail: For the first time, the council has added a £1.5m 'savings deliverability adjustment' to mitigate optimism bias and slippage risk on its £12m savings programme. This acknowledgement suggests the council has previously overestimated its ability to deliver savings.
findings.matters: If the council struggles to deliver £12m in new savings, the adjustment only covers £1.5m of shortfall, creating risk to the balanced budget
findings.figures: £1.5m savings deliverability adjustment on £12.0m total new savings proposals
findings.quote: Whilst robust due diligence has been undertaken, the risk exists that the identified savings may not be delivered due to circumstances beyond the Council's control and for the first time a savings adjustment has been built into the budget to mitigate optimism bias and slippage into future years.

findings.headline: Financial resilience classified as 'vulnerable', only aiming to reach 'stable' status in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council remains classified as 'vulnerable' under its Financial Resilience Framework, with an aim to reach 'stable' during 2026/27. The document notes that 'resilient' status is achievable only if the council maintains strict financial discipline, signalling the council has been under stress.
findings.matters: Vulnerable status indicates a history of financial stress; only strong execution prevents further deterioration
findings.figures: Current status: vulnerable; target for 2026/27: stable; aspirational: resilient
findings.quote: The Council's current financial resilience remains classed as 'vulnerable', with the aim of moving to 'stable' during 2026/27.

findings.headline: £5.4m temporary accommodation pressure with government subsidy cap preventing full cost recovery
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation faces £5.4m demand growth in 2026/27. The council is actively lobbying to lift the government's temporary accommodation subsidy cap, which the council estimates accounts for £10m of unmet pressure, indicating government funding does not cover actual costs.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a demand-led, rising pressure; the council is committed to housing people but the subsidy does not cover it
findings.figures: £5.4m budget growth for 2026/27; £10m total subsidy cap shortfall identified
findings.quote: The Council continues to lobby to lift the TA subsidy cap which accounts for £10m of the pressure and the raising of LHA to the 30% of the market on an ongoing basis.

findings.headline: £23m DSG deficit now covered 90% by government High Needs Stability grant, reducing council's cash drain
findings.detail: The council carries a £23m DSG deficit which previously cost £0.9m annually in interest. The government's new High Needs Stability grant will fund 90% of DSG deficits subject to conditions and Department for Education assessment. This materially improves the position if the council's deficit qualifies.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit has been a major draw on reserves; this grant removes most of that obligation, freeing resources for other pressures
findings.figures: £23m deficit; £0.9m annual interest cost at 3.85%; 90% coverage from new grant
findings.quote: The government announced in the final settlement a new High Needs Stability grant that will fund 90% of DSG deficits subject to conditions.

findings.headline: £25.3m combined adult and children's social care pressures from demographic demand and inflation
findings.detail: Adult Social Care faces £19.3m pressure from demographic demand, inflation, and bad debt provision. Children's Social Care faces £6.0m from inflation and external care purchasing demand. These are the largest identified growth items and reflect sector-wide demand acceleration.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led; if demand exceeds forecasts or inflation accelerates, overspends will quickly follow and reserves will be drawn
findings.figures: £19.3m Adult Social Care; £6.0m Children's Social Care
findings.quote: The most significant growth areas and pressures for 2026/27 are forecast to be: • £19.3m Adult Social Care from demographic demand, inflation, and Bad Debt Provision. • £6.0m Children's Social Care from inflation and demand for external care purchasing.

findings.headline: £34.5m cumulative budget gap in 2029/30-2030/31 with no identified funding solution specified
findings.detail: The council can balance budgets for 2026/27-2028/29 following the Fair Funding Review, but the MTFP shows a projected gap of £14.8m in 2029/30 and £19.7m in 2030/31, totalling £34.5m. The council states this gap is "expected to be met through savings, income and funding changes" but these are not detailed.
findings.matters: A £34.5m gap with unspecified mitigation means the council will need to deliver major savings or further cuts that are not yet planned
findings.figures: £34.5m cumulative gap; £14.8m in 2029/30 and £19.7m in 2030/31
findings.quote: Approve the latest General Fund Medium-Term Financial Plan estimates for 2026/27 to 2030/31 set out in Table 3 and to note the estimated budget gap of £34.5m at the end of that period.

findings.headline: £9.6m owed by NHS Integrated Care Board creates cash timing risk
findings.detail: As at 15 January 2026, the local NHS Integrated Care Board owes Enfield Council £9.6m. The council explicitly notes this affects its cash position ('The Council's cash position is also affected by non-payment of other debt'). The paper provides no clarity on the nature of the debt, its terms, or expected settlement date.
findings.matters: A £9.6m debtor owed by a government body creates cash flow timing risk. NHS entities are notoriously slow payers. If settlement is delayed, the council may need to draw on reserves or borrow short-term working capital to fund operations, increasing short-term borrowing costs.
findings.figures: ICB debt as at 15 January 2026: £9.6m; total gross investments 30 Nov 2025 £116.8m
findings.quote: as at 15 January 2026, the ICB (part of the NHS) owes the Council £9.6m.

findings.headline: Schools have £6.3m outstanding debt and recovery status is unclear
findings.detail: Fifteen schools owe Enfield Council £6.3m in licensed deficit agreements (temporary revenue support facilities). The paper states that 'The Council's Finance Team and Education Service are working with the schools to ensure the debts are recoverable and to establish the Council's exposure', language indicating that collection risk has not been fully quantified. Interest is charged at base rate + 1% and deducted from school advance payments.
findings.matters: While £6.3m is small relative to total council debt, the need to 'establish exposure' signals that recovery is not assured. School deficits often persist; if schools cannot repay, the council will either need to fund the deficits from revenue (increasing overspend risk) or write off the debt (reserves impact).
findings.figures: School debt 30 Nov 2025: £6.3m (15 schools); balance 1 Apr 2025 £6.4m; advances 8 months £0.7m, repayments £0.8m, net reduction £0.1m
findings.quote: The Council's Finance Team and Education Service are working with the schools to ensure the debts are recoverable and to establish the Council's exposure.

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs rising toward affordability ceiling
findings.detail: Enfield's General Fund capital financing costs as a proportion of Net Revenue Budget increased from 7.3% (2024/25 outturn) to 8.2% (Q3 2025/26 forecast). The council's approved target range is 10-12%, but the trajectory is material: a 0.9 percentage point rise in one year driven by lower investment income and higher Minimum Revenue Provision charges.
findings.matters: A rising debt-servicing ratio indicates declining financial headroom. If investment returns continue to fall (already down to 3.96% from 4.96% a year ago) and MRP pressures persist, the council could approach the upper affordability ceiling of 12%, constraining its ability to respond to emergencies or new borrowing needs.
findings.figures: General Fund capital financing costs as proportion of NRB: 7.3% (2024/25 outturn), 8.2% (2025/26 forecast); approved target range 10-12%
findings.quote: Debt Servicing costs as a proportion of Net Revenue Budget (NRB): An assessment of the sustainability of the Council's borrowing commitments in the context of its revenue resources. This limit was set 10% - 12%... The indicator for Q3 is 8.2% (2024/25 pre-audit 7.3%).

findings.headline: £181m contingent liability from North London Waste Authority debt exposure
findings.detail: Enfield is one of seven councils in the North London Waste Authority (NLWA), which holds £1.27bn of debt. If Enfield bears 1/7th of NLWA's debt (as illustrated in the paper), the equivalent exposure is approximately £181m. This contingent liability does not appear on the council's balance sheet but will flow through gate fees and council contributions if NLWA debt increases or if the authority struggles to refinance.
findings.matters: A £181m contingent liability is substantial relative to Enfield's £1.3bn direct debt. NLWA is currently holding short-term maturity debt awaiting refinancing to longer-term products 'when rates permit', creating refinancing risk. Any cost inflation will flow through to waste gate fees and increase Enfield's revenue pressure.
findings.figures: NLWA total debt £1.27bn (£230m below authorised limit); Enfield's 1/7th share approximately £181m; Enfield's 2025/26 NLWA contribution forecast £14.1m
findings.quote: As an illustration, if Enfield ultimately bears the cost of one seventh of the debt, Enfield's share of risk is the equivalent to £181m of debt.

findings.headline: £55.7m Energetik loans at risk if Meridian Water or HRA regeneration schemes slip
findings.detail: The council has advanced £55.7m to Energetik (its heat network subsidiary) comprising capital and revenue loans. The paper explicitly states that delays in Meridian Water or HRA regeneration scheme completion will adversely affect Energetik's ability to service these loans, potentially triggering unbudgeted Expected Credit Loss (ECL) charges. The earmarked reserve is £1.9m but the council is only adding £200k in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Energetik's business model depends on property development schemes which are often subject to market, planning, and cost pressures. Delays to either scheme will impair Energetik's cash flow and ability to repay, creating a second-order risk to the council's General Fund via ECL provisions or loan loss.
findings.figures: Energetik loans 30 Nov 2025 £55.7m (up from £51.7m on 1 Apr 2025); advances Apr-Nov 2025 £5.5m, repayments £1.5m; Energetik Shareholder reserve £1.9m (31 Mar 2025) with £200k budgeted addition
findings.quote: Changes in the Meridian Water and HRA regeneration schemes may adversely affect the ability of Energetik to repay its loans which may result in additional charges for ECLs to the Council's General Fund.

findings.headline: HRA concessionary borrowing rate (40bps discount) expires 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The council currently borrows HRA debt at PWLB rates minus 40bps under a time-limited government concession. This expires in March 2027. Once expired, HRA borrowing will return to standard PWLB rates (20-year currently 6.04%) which are 60bps higher than current HRA rates, creating a known cost shock in less than 12 months.
findings.matters: The expiry date is fixed and the cost impact is material. With HRA debt forecast to grow and ICR already below minimum, higher borrowing rates will worsen affordability precisely when the HRA has no capacity to absorb the cost increase.
findings.figures: Current HRA borrowing rate 4.6% (with 40bps concession); PWLB 20-year standard rate 6.04% as at 30 Nov 2025; current General Fund rate 5.00%
findings.quote: This concessionary rate is currently in place only until March 2027.

findings.headline: HRA debt will not reduce and is exposed to long-term interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account debt is forecast to grow from £427.9m (2024/25) to £536.3m (2027/28) and is not forecast to decline. This leaves the HRA permanently exposed to interest rate movements, unable to use debt reduction as a hedge against future rate rises, unlike the General Fund which uses internal borrowing.
findings.matters: A growing HRA debt balance with no reduction pathway is vulnerable to rate shocks. With the HRA concessionary borrowing rate (40bps discount) ending March 2027, higher rates will compound the affordability squeeze already evident in the falling ICR.
findings.quote: The HRA is relatively more exposed to interest rate risk in the long term as the absolute debt is not forecast to reduce.

findings.headline: HRA Interest Cover Ratio forecast to fall below its prudential minimum
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's Interest Cover Ratio is forecast at 1.25 for 2025/26, below the council's own minimum target of 1.60. This measures the adequacy of operating surplus to cover interest costs and signals that the HRA's revenue buffer to absorb interest or other shocks is shrinking. This follows a 2024/25 outturn of 1.71.
findings.matters: An ICR falling below minimum indicates the HRA's operating margin is compressing and cannot absorb further interest rate rises or revenue shortfalls without drawing on reserves or cutting investment. This threatens the sustainability of the council's largest debt portfolio (£464m of £1.47bn total).
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio 2024/25 outturn 1.71; 2025/26 forecast 1.25; minimum target 1.60
findings.quote: Interest Cover Ratio (ICR) Measures adequacy of the in-year revenue surplus to cover interest on borrowing Calculated as: Operating surplus divided by interest costs 1.71 1.25 minimum 1.60

findings.paper_title: KD 5956 - Housing Delivery and Placemaking Ten Year Plan and SAHP Bid 26-36 Part 1 FINAL
findings.headline: Council faces material and accelerating housing crisis with 3,000+ in temporary accommodation and 500 monthly homelessness approaches
findings.detail: Enfield reports over 7,000 households on the Housing Register and more than 3,000 living in temporary accommodation. Homelessness approaches average 500 per month, 'a figure that has increased dramatically in recent years.' The council operates a national placement policy for temporary housing due to capacity constraints. This scale of unmet demand drives the 10-year programme ambition.
findings.matters: Quantifies the underlying housing and homelessness crisis driving Enfield's borrowing and grant dependency decisions. Temporary accommodation is expensive revenue pressure on the General Fund. Underdelivery against the 10-year plan would leave the council unable to address statutory homelessness duties and continue expensive out-of-borough placements.
findings.figures: 7,000+ households on Housing Register; 3,000+ in temporary accommodation; 500 homelessness approaches per month (increased dramatically); average house prices exceed £450,000; private rents consuming over 40% of household income
findings.quote: Over 7,000 households are currently on the Housing Register, and more than 3,000 are living in temporary accommodation. The Council receives on average 500 homelessness approaches per month, a figure that has increased dramatically in recent years.

findings.paper_title: KD 5956 - Housing Delivery and Placemaking Ten Year Plan and SAHP Bid 26-36 Part 1 FINAL
findings.headline: HRA will increase borrowing to support the 10-year housing delivery programme
findings.detail: The programme approval states 'Borrowing increases are manageable within HRA, financial metrics remain within approved thresholds.' However, the specific amount of increased borrowing is not disclosed in this public report. Critically, this borrowing increase is contingent on achieving minimum grant rates from the GLA; if grants fall short, borrowing would need to increase further.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility to the council's borrowing trajectory and debt metrics. The 'manageable' statement is qualified by the conditional viability statement. If GLA grant rates fall below expectations, HRA borrowing would need to increase materially, potentially affecting debt service cover and other metrics lenders monitor.
findings.figures: Existing £200m grant deployed for 1,100 homes; specific borrowing increase amounts not disclosed in Part 1; financial metrics stated to 'remain within approved thresholds'
findings.quote: Borrowing increases are manageable within HRA, financial metrics remain within approved thresholds, and risks are mitigated through appropriate contingencies and governance controls.

findings.paper_title: KD 5956 - Housing Delivery and Placemaking Ten Year Plan and SAHP Bid 26-36 Part 1 FINAL
findings.headline: Council plans programme contingency to manage unforeseen costs, delays, and market volatility
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies delivery risks and states 'A programme contingency will be included in our Business Plan to protect delivery against unforeseen costs, delays, or market volatility.' The financial implications emphasize that 'Ongoing financial modelling, sensitivity testing and oversight will be essential' given dependency on 'inflation, and market conditions.' The specific contingency amount and proportion of total programme cost are not disclosed in this public part.
findings.matters: Signals the council recognizes material cost inflation, schedule delay, and market volatility risks in a large 10-year capital programme. The contingency acknowledgement suggests planned cost headroom, but lack of disclosed quantum limits lender visibility into whether risk mitigation is proportionate to programme scale.
findings.figures: £200m grant already deployed; specific contingency amount and percentage not disclosed in Part 1
findings.quote: A programme contingency will be included in our Business Plan to protect delivery against unforeseen costs, delays, or market volatility.

findings.paper_title: KD 5956 - Housing Delivery and Placemaking Ten Year Plan and SAHP Bid 26-36 Part 1 FINAL
findings.headline: Housing programme viability depends on GLA negotiating grant rates at or above minimum modelled levels
findings.detail: The council explicitly conditions financial viability on achieving minimum grant rates: 'The proposed programme is affordable, financially viable and aligned with the approved HRA Business Plan, provided grant is secured at or above minimum modelled levels.' The council will negotiate with the GLA on grant rates necessary to create a viable programme, with a separate Cabinet report to follow negotiation. This makes the financial model contingent on negotiation outcomes.
findings.matters: For lenders, Enfield's approved financial position could change materially depending on GLA negotiation outcomes. The 10-year plan, which involves significant borrowing increases, is contingent on achieving specific grant rates. Failure to achieve minimum rates would force either plan revision or increased HRA borrowing.
findings.figures: £200m of grant funding already secured for 1,100 affordable homes; total programme targeting 3,000 homes; up to £11.7bn available across London for SAHP; homes must start by March 2036
findings.quote: The proposed programme is affordable, financially viable and aligned with the approved HRA Business Plan, provided grant is secured at or above minimum modelled levels.

findings.headline: MRP methodology changed from fixed 3.50% to prevailing PWLB rate to reflect current cost of borrowing
findings.detail: The Council has adopted a revised Minimum Revenue Provision policy, changing the annuity rate for unsupported borrowing from a fixed 3.50% to the prevailing PWLB rate. This follows an independent review by CIPFA in February 2025 and better aligns debt repayment to actual borrowing costs.
findings.matters: MRP policy changes affect pace of debt repayment; moving to market-based rates signals recognition that fixed assumptions no longer reflect reality
findings.figures: MRP rate change from fixed 3.50% to prevailing PWLB rate
findings.quote: Change in the annuity rate used for Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) applied to unsupported borrowing from 2026/27 from the fixed 3.50% to the prevailing PWLB rate to better reflect the Council's cost of borrowing.

findings.headline: Council in top quartile for debt-to-capacity and implementing multi-year deleveraging plan to reach third quartile by 2028/29
findings.detail: Enfield's debt, when scaled to its financial capacity, is currently in the top quartile compared to similar councils. The Council's debt strategy aims to move to the third quartile by 2028/29 by constraining General Fund borrowing at £997m (2024/25 level). This acknowledged overleveraging is driving a staged debt reduction plan.
findings.matters: High leverage relative to peers indicates financial stress; a constrained borrowing cap suggests limited capacity for new commitments or shocks
findings.figures: General Fund borrowing capped at £997m; targeting movement from top to third quartile by 2028/29
findings.quote: Keeping the Capital Financing Requirement at 2024/25 levels is likely to be sufficient to bring Enfield from the top quartile to the third quartile for 'debt scaled to size of local authority' by 2028/29

findings.headline: Capital financing costs increasing by £3.4m (13% increase) from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.detail: General Fund capital financing revenue costs are forecast to increase by £3.4m from £28.9m in 2025/26 to £32.3m in 2026/27, driven by higher interest rate assumptions. Total capital financing cost remains within the Council's 10-12% affordability range at 7.2% of net revenue budget, but the trend is upward.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce revenue budget flexibility for services and indicate vulnerability if interest rates rise further
findings.figures: Capital financing cost rising from £28.9m to £32.3m (+£3.4m); now 7.2% of net revenue budget
findings.quote: The 2026/27 General Fund revenue cost for capital financing is forecast to increase by £3.4m from £28.9m in 2025/26 to £32.3m in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Meridian Water capital receipts downgraded by £270m over ten years due to weaker market conditions
findings.detail: Capital receipts from the Meridian Water development have been prudently re-profiled downward by approximately £270m over the next ten years, due to current weaker development market conditions. This means debt will reduce more slowly than previously planned and forecast debt position at the end of the next ten years is now higher than estimated twelve months ago.
findings.matters: Delay in capital receipts means slower debt reduction and higher debt levels than previously forecast, increasing refinancing risk and financial pressure over the medium term
findings.figures: £270m reduction in anticipated Meridian Water capital receipts over next ten years
findings.quote: Weaker market conditions mean that expected capital receipts have been delayed and may ultimately be lower than previously forecast. Over the next ten years, the revised profile reduces anticipated receipts by £270m.

findings.headline: Refinancing risk: £49.8m of existing debt must be refinanced at 4.90% versus current cost of 3.18%, creating £860k additional annual cost
findings.detail: The Council must refinance £49.8m of existing debt in 2026/27 at the new rate of 4.90%, compared to the existing average cost of 3.18%. This represents a refinancing risk as the difference costs an additional £860k annually. New borrowing is assumed at 4.9%, significantly higher than the current weighted average of 3.18%.
findings.matters: Rising refinancing costs directly impact debt serviceability and reduce financial capacity; lenders assess vulnerability to interest rate rises
findings.figures: £49.8m refinancing at 4.90% vs 3.18%; annual additional cost £860k; new borrowing assumption 4.9%
findings.quote: After providing MRP of £19.8m, the remaining £49.8m will have to be funded by re-borrowing at higher rates of 4.90%. This re-borrowing is required to repay historic debt costing 3.18% on average. As an illustration, the annual difference in interest of borrowing £49.8m at estimated 4.90% rather than 3.18% is £860k.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: Awaab's Law (mandatory damp and mould standards) compliance effective October 2025 adds unbudgeted regulatory cost pressure
findings.detail: The paper identifies mandatory damp and mould standards under Awaab's Law (effective October 2025) as one of the 'significant challenges' driving HRA pressures. This is treated as a cost driver within the capital and revenue investment programmes but represents an unfunded mandate driving investment requirements.
findings.matters: New regulatory compliance requirement increases investment needs and cost base; compliance failure carries reputational and enforcement risk
findings.figures: Building Safety investment programme includes costs; no separate quantification of Awaab's Law incremental costs provided
findings.quote: Mandatory damp and mould standards under Awaab's Law (effective October 2025)

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: Right-to-Buy sales forecast collapsed from 150 to 20 units annually following October 2024 policy changes
findings.detail: Following the Autumn 2024 Budget announcement reducing RTB maximum discounts from £136,400 to £16,000, the council's RTB sales forecast has dropped dramatically to 20 units per year (from 150). While the government has extended indefinite 100% retention of RTB receipts for replacement homes, the lower sales volume means less capital receipts available for the acquisition and investment programme.
findings.matters: Significant reduction in discretionary capital receipts; the council will need to rely more heavily on borrowing and grant funding to deliver development targets
findings.figures: RTB sales forecast: 150 units (previous assumption) → 20 units (proposed); historical spend programme: £35.8m over next 5 years (but now spread over fewer properties)
findings.quote: The impact of these changes in the short term has seen an increase in capital receipts from sales in 2025-26 and potentially into 2026-27. However, significantly fewer sales are predicted after that.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA concessionary borrowing rate expires June 2026; forward rates assumed at 5% average versus current 4.9%
findings.detail: Central Government's 0.4% discount on HRA borrowing rates (which has been extended multiple times) is currently due to expire June 2026. The council is expecting an update in January 2026 to confirm continuation, but forward planning assumes rates rise to 5% average. If rates are not extended, refinancing costs will increase.
findings.matters: Unresolved refinancing exposure; if concessionary rates are withdrawn and forward rates apply, debt service costs increase at a time when the plan is already dependent on achieving savings targets
findings.figures: Current average borrowing rate 4.9% (as of 31/12/2025); forward assumed rate 5% average; concessionary discount 0.4%
findings.quote: The Council will continue to borrow at the HRA concessionary rates to support the HRA until the concessionary rate expires, this is in accordance with the Treasury Strategy. We are expecting an update in January 2026 to confirm whether HRA concessionary rates will continue past March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: Predicted 21% electricity and 15% gas charge increases from 2026 reflect significant energy cost inflation embedded in HRA costs
findings.detail: The current Housing energy contract (secured until September 2026) will be replaced with charges expected to rise by average 21% for electricity and 15% for gas from October 2026. The paper attributes this to non-commodity charges including grid infrastructure improvements and regulatory adjustments. While tenants bear these charges directly, they reflect the underlying cost base the HRA is exposed to.
findings.matters: Energy cost inflation is a major pass-through cost pressure; if tenant affordability deteriorates, could drive rent arrears and collection risk
findings.figures: Electricity: average 21% increase from October 2026; Gas: average 15% increase from April 2026
findings.quote: tenants will experience an average energy increase of 21% in the 2026-27 charges. The current Housing energy contract was secured until September 2026 and from October 26, the charges are expected to increase

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA reserves being drawn down to minimum prudent level; balance drops £6.6m to £9.3m
findings.detail: The HRA Balance (general reserves) are forecast to drop from £15.9m to £9.3m, a planned drawdown of £6.6m. This leaves the council with only £0.3m headroom above its minimum requirement of £9.57m (10% of turnover). The paper describes this as 'planned' but notes 'balances will not go below this level' and the position is 'within the HRA's minimum requirement'.
findings.matters: Limited buffer for unforeseen pressures (energy costs, regulatory changes, delivery delays); any adverse variance in income or costs could breach minimum reserve policy
findings.figures: HRA Balance: £15.9m (01/04/2025) → £9.3m (01/04/2026); minimum required £9.57m; headroom £0.3m
findings.quote: The estimated remaining level is within the HRA's minimum requirement of 10% of turnover £9.57m

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: Efficiency savings of £1m annually are a critical dependency for financial viability; not achieving them would breach Interest Cover Ratio target
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that the Interest Cover Ratio of 1.85 (which demonstrates the HRA can service debt) is 'dependent on the revenue budget achieving the proposed savings as set out in the revenue section of this report.' These £1m annual Management and Maintenance efficiencies are built into the plan through 2028-29. The paper notes 'at a time of pro-active regulation, the sector faces challenges in managing within a reduced cost envelope' and identifies this as a key financial risk.
findings.matters: If £1m efficiency savings are not achieved, the HRA's key affordability metric (ICR of 1.25 minimum) would be at risk; this is an executability risk on a forecasted rather than proven programme
findings.figures: £1m per annum efficiency required; ICR 1.85 baseline requires these savings to maintain above 1.25 minimum
findings.quote: remaining above the recommended level is dependent on the revenue budget achieving the proposed savings as set out in the revenue section of this report

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 HRA Budget Setting Report and Business Plan 2026/27
findings.headline: Loan-to-Value ratio exceeds approved benchmarks for three years due to development borrowing programme
findings.detail: LTV is forecast to peak at 54% in 2026/27 against the council's own 50% maximum benchmark, and will remain above this for 2027/28 and 2028/29. This is being driven by £141m borrowing over 10 years to deliver the Affordable Homes development programme. The council acknowledges this 'brings an increased level of exposure to interest rate changes' and proposes to mitigate this by building a capital financing reserve and completing developments quickly to generate rental income.
findings.matters: Leverage exceeding internal policy benchmarks signals higher refinancing and interest rate risk; the mitigation (completing homes quickly and maintaining reserve) depends on delivery execution
findings.figures: LTV peaks at 54% in 2026/27 (forecast to fall to 50% by 2029/30); £141m borrowing over 10 years; opening debt £463.9m rising to £604.9m by 2031/32
findings.quote: peaking at 54% loan to value brings an increased level of exposure to interest rate changes. To mitigate this, the HRA will build its own capital financing reserve and will also tightly manage the development programme so that homes are completed and tenanted as quickly as possible.

findings.headline: Two changes of S151 Officer and CEO within the reporting period; recruitment challenges across finance team
findings.detail: Senior financial leadership stability has been poor. The council experienced turnover in the S151 Officer role, CEO, Leader, and General Purposes Committee Chair. Within the finance function there were recruitment challenges and vacancies throughout 2024/25. The auditor noted that a significant number of permanent appointments were made at senior finance level after year-end, and that maintaining skilled resources should be treated as a priority given the complexity of financial issues the council faces.
findings.matters: Frequent changes in senior finance leadership and persistent vacancies increase execution risk on financial strategies and weaken control environment. For a lender, this suggests capacity constraints in delivering the necessary financial improvements.
findings.figures: Changes to S151 Officer, CFO, CEO, Leader, and General Purposes Committee Chair; permanent appointments made post-year-end
findings.quote: There has been a turnover in senior leadership roles, including the section 151 Officer, the Chief Executive Officer, the Leader and the General Purposes Committee Chair. Within Finance, the Council had to deal with recruitment challenge and vacancies during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Corporate Risk Register was not reported to governance during 2024/25; Internal Audit delivery dropped 60 percent
findings.detail: Governance over risk management weakened during 2024/25. Neither the Corporate Risk Register nor a Risk Management Strategy were shared with the General Purposes Committee during 2024/25, despite this being standard practice across local government (typically quarterly). Additionally, Internal Audit delivered only 14 assurance opinions in 2024/25 compared to 34 in 2022/23 — a 60 percent reduction. The auditor identified this as a significant weakness in governance.
findings.matters: Absence of formal risk reporting to members and reduced internal audit coverage reduce the council's ability to identify and manage emerging problems. For a lender, this suggests weaker early-warning systems for financial or operational deterioration.
findings.figures: Internal Audit: 14 assurance opinions in 2024/25 vs 34 in 2022/23
findings.quote: Neither the Corporate Risk Register nor the Risk Management Strategy were shared with the General Purposes Committee during 2024/25.

findings.headline: Auditor likely to issue Disclaimer Opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to lack of assurance over opening balances
findings.detail: The council has not had audited accounts since December 2019 (for 2018/19). The previous auditors (BDO) did not sign an opinion from 2019/20 onwards and did not complete value-for-money work under the NAO Code until 2025. The 2024/25 audit is ongoing and Grant Thornton has indicated they are likely to issue a Disclaimer Audit Opinion due to lack of assurance over opening balances. Work on in-year transactions and closing balances is still ongoing.
findings.matters: Inability to audit opening balances for a full year undermines confidence in the accuracy of reported balances and transactions. Six years without audited accounts is highly unusual and signals prior governance or financial reporting difficulties. For a lender, this represents a material information risk.
findings.figures: No audited accounts since December 2019; previous auditor gap from 2019/20 to 2022/23
findings.quote: Our audit of your financial statements is ongoing at the time of issuing this Interim Auditor's Annual Report, however we are very likely issue a Disclaimer Audit Opinion in respect of the 2024-25 Accounts due to the lack of assurance over the opening balances.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision policy changes to add £19 million per annum to annual debt servicing costs from 2025/26
findings.detail: CIPFA recommended in February 2025 that the council align its MRP (minimum revenue provision) policy to the standard approach. From 2025/26 onwards, the council's annual MRP charge is expected to rise to £19 million per annum. CIPFA noted that the policy used in previous years for loans to third parties differed from the standard approach, and those accounts have not yet been audited. This represents a significant structural increase in the annual debt cost.
findings.matters: A £19m per annum addition to fixed debt costs represents a material increase to the council's budget requirement and reduces financial flexibility. The fact that prior-year accounting treatment may differ from standard suggests possible restatement risk once prior accounts are audited.
findings.figures: £19 million per annum MRP charge from 2025/26 onwards
findings.quote: From 2025/26 onwards, following CIPFA recommendations made in February 2025, the Council's annual minimum revenue provision (MRP) charge is expected to rise to £19 million per annum.

findings.headline: Meridian Water project faces loss of £195 million Housing Infrastructure Fund grant if delayed beyond November 2026
findings.detail: The council's major regeneration project carries significant delivery risk. Meridian Water is the largest of the council's debt-financed projects with £379.8 million capital financing requirement. The project is already running late due to infrastructure and engineering issues identified after planning. If the project falls further behind schedule and is delayed beyond November 2026, the council risks having to repay £195 million of Housing Infrastructure Fund grant funding to MHCLG. The capital value of work to date (£547 million) includes £63.9 million of capitalised interest that will only be recoverable if assets sell at rates covering all costs.
findings.matters: Project delay creates the potential for a sudden major liability (£195m grant repayment) and raises questions about asset values and capitalised costs. If Meridian Water assets do not sell at assumed prices, the council could face impairment losses.
findings.figures: £195 million Housing Infrastructure Fund at risk if delayed beyond November 2026; £379.8 million capital financing requirement; £547 million capital value to date including £63.9 million capitalised interest
findings.quote: The pace of progress on the Meridian Water project is also a risk for the Council. The project is already running late because of infrastructural issues identified after planning, but any delay now beyond November 2026 could technically result in £195 million of Housing Infrastructure Fund monies being repayable to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).

findings.headline: £63.4 million budget gap forecast for 2026/27 to 2029/30 with no central transformation programme to close it
findings.detail: The council faces a substantial medium-term budget gap with limited planning in place to close it. The 2025/26 budget itself is balanced only through £18.1 million of forecast savings and £5 million of reserve use, with £10 million of exceptional financial support approved in principle. Looking ahead, a £63.4 million gap is forecast between 2026/27 and 2029/30. The council has no central corporate transformation strategy and instead relies on ad-hoc 'savings weeks' and one-off opportunities rather than recurring initiatives.
findings.matters: A large multi-year budget gap with no credible transformation plan to close it suggests the council will need either further exceptional support or service reductions. For a lender, this indicates medium-term financial stress.
findings.figures: £63.4 million budget gap forecast 2026/27 to 2029/30; £18.1 million savings in 2025/26 budget; £5 million reserve use in 2025/26
findings.quote: There is a forecast budget gap of a further £63.4 million between 2026/27 and 2029/30.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased 30 percent in one year despite offsetting adjustments at year-end
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is a significant and growing pressure. In Quarter 3 of 2024/25 the forecast overspend against the high needs block was £4.5 million, taking the cumulative deficit from £14.752 million to £19.252 million — a 30 percent increase. Although the actual year-end deficit was recorded as £17.4 million following identification of offsetting monies, the underlying overspend on high needs remained at £4.5 million. The auditor identified this as a significant weakness in arrangements and there is uncertainty about what can or cannot be charged to the DSG budget.
findings.matters: A growing ring-fenced deficit that the council cannot offset from general resources is a material pressure on future budgets. The auditor's finding that there are questions about charging and staffing gaps in this area suggests the position could worsen.
findings.figures: DSG deficit increased from £14.752 million to forecast £19.252 million in Q3 2024/25 (30 percent increase); actual year-end £17.4 million; underlying high needs overspend £4.5 million
findings.quote: In Quarter 3 of 2024/25, the Council was forecast to overspend against the 2024/25 budget by £4.5 million - taking the deficit on the account from £14.752 million to £19.252 million. This was a 30% increase in the value of the deficit.

findings.headline: Risk reserves of £32.4 million are £10.6 million below the assessed minimum threshold of £43 million and £50.6 million below the target of £83 million
findings.detail: The council's financial resilience is weakened by reserves below minimum safe levels. The council holds £32.441 million in risk reserves but has assessed its minimum acceptable threshold at £43 million and its target threshold at £83 million. This leaves the council vulnerable to unexpected costs or revenue pressures without having to request further exceptional financial support.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb budget shocks and indicate reliance on government exceptional financial support to maintain liquidity. For a lender, this signals constrained capacity to manage unexpected adverse movements.
findings.figures: £32.441 million held; £43 million minimum threshold; £83 million target threshold
findings.quote: On 31 March 2025, the Council held risk reserves of £32.441 million. The Council has assessed that its risk reserves are low. It assesses that that the minimum threshold should be £43 million, but that the target threshold for 2025/26 is £83 million.

findings.headline: General Fund debt of £1.286 billion rising to £1.5 billion by end 2025/26, with annual servicing costs of £31.4 million growing by £4 million per annum
findings.detail: The council's debt position has grown significantly and is expected to continue rising. The net cost of General Fund debt for 2025/26 is £31.4 million and is expected to grow by another £4 million per annum in 2026/27 and 2027/28. This is a major structural cost pressure on the budget. The debt includes £51.715 million to Energetik Ltd, £141.902 million to Housing Gateway Ltd, and £379.8 million capital financing requirement for Meridian Water.
findings.matters: High debt levels and rising debt servicing costs constrain the council's financial flexibility and ability to invest in services. For a lender, this represents a growing first-charge claim on the council's resources.
findings.figures: £1.286 billion debt at 31 March 2025; expected £1.5 billion by end 2025/26; £31.4 million net cost 2025/26 rising by £4 million per annum
findings.quote: The Council had debts of £1.286 billion at the end of 2024/25. £429 million related to the Housing Revenue Account, the rest to the General Fund. The Council expects to have debts of £1.5 billion by the end of 2025/26 (of which, £467 million will relate to the Housing Revenue Account, with the balance being General Fund). The estimated net cost of General Fund debt for 2025/26 is £31.4 million, but this is expected to grow by another £4 million per annum in 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.headline: Management inquiry responses delayed by 9 months: submitted March 2025, received December 2025.
findings.detail: Auditors submitted standard management inquiry letters in March 2025 requesting information about fraud risk, related parties and regulatory compliance. Responses were only received in early December 2025, approximately nine months after issue. These inquiries are critical for risk assessment and their timely completion is necessary for an efficient and effective audit.
findings.matters: Such significant delays in providing auditor inquiries suggest weak finance function processes and governance oversight, and indicate an overstretched finance team unable to prioritise audit cooperation.
findings.figures: Inquiries issued March 2025; responses received early December 2025; approximately 9 months delay
findings.quote: Management inquiries were submitted in March 2025 and were only received back from the Council in early December, which is nearly nine months after these were issued to the Council.

findings.headline: Final accounts not produced until 2 October 2025, leaving insufficient time for rigorous audit testing before statutory backstop date of 28 February 2026.
findings.detail: Although draft accounts met the 30 June 2025 statutory deadline, the published version required significant redrafting (PPE, MIRS, cash flow, group accounts). The final revised accounts were not available until early October 2025. Due to timing and the backstop deadline, auditors were unable to complete sufficient audit procedures on key areas including closing asset valuations, cash flow statement, MIRS, group accounts, debtors and creditors.
findings.matters: Late-produced accounts prevent thorough independent audit review before they are finalised, increasing the risk of material undetected errors and preventing the auditors from providing meaningful assurance to users.
findings.figures: Draft deadline 30 June 2025; final revision 2 October 2025; backstop deadline 28 February 2026
findings.quote: Although the Council published its draft accounts by the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025, the accounts required significant redrafting, including revisions to PPE, the Movement in Reserves Statement (MIRS), cash flow, and Group financial statements. The final revised version was not available until 2 October 2025, which limited the time available for rigorous review and completion of audit procedures.

findings.headline: S151 Officer turnover and 30% increase in Dedicated Schools Grant deficit add to financial risk.
findings.detail: Leadership changes including the departure of the s151 Officer (the council's chief financial officer) occur at a time when the council faces acute financial stress. Simultaneously, the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased by 30%, adding a new material financial pressure and reducing the council's flexibility to reallocate resources.
findings.matters: Loss of senior financial leadership during a crisis period creates execution risk for the recovery plan and signals internal instability; the DSG pressure is a non-discretionary cost that further squeezes the general fund.
findings.figures: 30% increase in Dedicated Schools Grant deficit
findings.quote: Leadership turnover, including the s151 Officer, and a 30% increase in the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit add to financial risk.

findings.headline: Auditors issued a Statutory Recommendation requiring the council to agree and implement options to reduce debt and annual servicing costs.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton issued a formal Statutory Recommendation under Section 24 Schedule 7 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014, accepted by Full Council on 12 November 2025. The council must agree and implement options to reduce debt and annual servicing costs, prioritise de-risking of major projects, and rebuild risk reserves to at least £43 million by end of 2026-27.
findings.matters: A Statutory Recommendation is a formal regulatory requirement that signals auditor judgment that the council has failed to put proper arrangements in place to secure value for money, and non-compliance with it can trigger regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: Recommendation accepted 12 November 2025; target £43 million reserves by end 2026-27; target £83 million by 2026-27
findings.quote: Statutory Recommendation (accepted by Full Council on 12 Nov 2025): Agree and implement options to reduce debt and annual servicing costs, prioritising de-risking of major projects. Progress actions to rebuild risk reserves to at least £43 million and work toward the £83 million target by end of 2026/27, focusing on recurring savings to avoid reliance on exceptional support.

findings.headline: Council using annuity method for MRP which defers charges to later years, understating current cost of borrowing by approximately £3.95 million.
findings.detail: The council applies the annuity method for calculating MRP, which front-loads lower charges and defers larger charges to future years, rather than the Useful Economic Life method which would result in more consistent annual charges. The auditors estimate this deferral understates the 2024-25 MRP charge by £3.95 million, and if UEL method were used the undercharge would be £8 million.
findings.matters: The chosen MRP method artificially improves current-year finances but worsens future-year deficits, masking the true cost of borrowing and creating unsustainable future budget pressures for the next administration.
findings.figures: £3.95 million 2024-25 undercharge; £8 million total undercharge if UEL method used
findings.quote: The Council currently applies the annuity method for MRP, which defers a significant portion of the charge to later years and understates the current cost of borrowing. We recommend that the Council disclose the long-term impact of this approach and consider updating the MRP note about this assumption, the difference notes above of £3.95 million is not material.

findings.headline: MRP model overstates Capital Financing Requirement by approximately £16 million compared to financial statements.
findings.detail: A fundamental flaw in the council's MRP model means the calculated CFR does not reconcile to the financial statements, creating uncertainty about whether MRP charges are correct. This discrepancy impacts the reliability of financial planning and raises questions about the accuracy of the council's debt management estimates.
findings.matters: The inability to reconcile the MRP model to the accounts is a control failure that undermines confidence in the accuracy of debt servicing calculations and suggests either the model or the accounts (or both) contain errors.
findings.figures: £16 million discrepancy between MRP model CFR and financial statements
findings.quote: Our review identified a flaw in the current MRP model, which overstates the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) by approximately £16 million compared to the financial statements. This impacts the reliability of the model and could lead to incorrect MRP charges and misinformed financial planning.

findings.headline: No MRP charged on £173 million of intercompany loans including to Energetik, creating estimated undercharge of £4.1 million.
findings.detail: The council has failed to apply Minimum Revenue Provision on £173 million of loans to subsidiaries, particularly to Energetik (an energy company), inconsistent with updated MRP guidance effective for 2024-25. Additionally, £5 million of share capital is funded by borrowing with no MRP charged. Energetik carries high credit risk and uncertain viability, creating significant financial exposure if loans are not repaid.
findings.matters: This represents both a breach of statutory MRP guidance and an undisclosed contingent liability; if Energetik cannot repay its loans, the council faces a major write-down and must absorb the loss from already-strained finances.
findings.figures: £173 million intercompany loans; £4.1 million estimated undercharge; £5 million share capital funded by debt
findings.quote: The Council has not applied Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) on intercompany loans totalling £173 million , including loans to Energetik, which is inconsistent with the latest MRP guidance effective for 2024/25. We estimate an undercharge of £4.1 million using the straight-line method. Moreover, Energetik carries high credit risk and uncertain viability, creating significant financial exposure if loans are not repaid.

findings.headline: Exceptional financial support of £20 million for 2024-25 and £10 million for 2025-26 has been agreed.
findings.detail: The council is dependent on exceptional government support to balance its budget in two consecutive years, indicating structural financial problems that cannot be resolved through normal budget management. This support is exceptional and discretionary, not a reliable funding source.
findings.matters: Reliance on exceptional support signals that the council's recurring income does not cover recurring expenditure and that the underlying financial position is unsustainable without extraordinary intervention.
findings.figures: £20 million 2024-25; £10 million 2025-26
findings.quote: Exceptional financial support has been agreed in principle (£20 million for 2024-25 and £10 million for 2025-26).

findings.headline: Risk reserves are critically low at £32.4 million versus minimum threshold of £43 million and target of £83 million.
findings.detail: The council has materially inadequate reserves relative to both the minimum prudent level and the target level. At end March 2025 reserves stood at £32.441 million, falling short of the minimum £43 million threshold and the 2025-26 target of £83 million. This severely constrains the council's ability to absorb any financial shocks or budget variations.
findings.matters: Insufficient reserves mean the council has minimal buffer for unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls and cannot absorb the type of in-year pressures that force exceptional support requests.
findings.figures: £32.441 million actual; £43 million minimum threshold; £83 million 2025-26 target
findings.quote: Risk reserves are low—£32.441 million at 31 March 2025 versus a minimum threshold of £43 million and a target of £83 million for 2025-26.

findings.headline: Council debt is significant and growing: £1.286 billion at end of 2024-25, projected to rise to £1.5 billion by 2025-26.
findings.detail: General Fund debt is £857 million, HRA debt is £429 million. The net cost of General Fund debt is estimated at £31.4 million for 2025-26, with annual increases of £4 million in 2026-27 and 2027-28. The council's ability to manage this debt is directly relevant to repayment capacity and financial sustainability.
findings.matters: The combination of growing absolute debt, rising annual servicing costs, and depleted reserves creates a trajectory toward unsustainability and signals increasing risk of default or need for further exceptional support.

findings.quote: The Council's debt position is significant and growing: £1.286 billion at the end of 2024/25 (£429 million HRA, remainder General Fund), projected to rise to £1.5 billion by 2025/26 (£467 million HRA). The net cost of General Fund debt is estimated at £31.4 million for 2025/26, increasing by £4 million annually in 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.headline: Auditors planning to issue a disclaimer of audit opinion, unable to form an opinion on financial statements.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton will issue a disclaimer of audit opinion for 2024-25 due to lack of assurance over opening balances from prior year's backstop-related disclaimer. The auditors have no assurance over closing reserves and were unable to complete sufficient work on key balance sheet items due to late production of final accounts in October 2025.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion is the most serious audit outcome short of a qualified opinion and signals fundamental uncertainty about the accuracy of the council's financial position, making it extremely high-risk for lenders.
